items.title: Academic Freedom Now: Rights, Classrooms, and the Future of Democratic Knowledge
items.excerpt: This panel examines academic freedom not only as an individual right, but as a collective condition necessary for the production, circulation, and contestation of knowledge within democratic societies. In alignment with the theme of Empowering Communities, we consider how academic freedom enables communities-within and beyond the university-to participate...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines academic freedom not only as an individual right, but as a collective condition necessary for the production, circulation, and contestation of knowledge within democratic societies. In alignment with the theme of Empowering Communities, we consider how academic freedom enables communities-within and beyond the university-to participate in processes of inquiry, critique, and meaning-making. The panel is structured around three interconnected vantage points. First, it addresses academic freedom as a legal and institutional framework, tracing its historical development and examining contemporary challenges, including policy restrictions, political pressures, and shifts in governance. Second, it considers the classroom as a site where academic freedom is enacted, negotiated, and sometimes constrained, focusing on pedagogical practices that foster open dialogue, critical engagement, and the capacity to navigate disagreement. Third, it explores the future of academic freedom in a changing political and technological landscape, asking how institutions, educators, and communities might work to sustain and rebuild conditions for intellectual autonomy and democratic participation. Across these perspectives, the panel foregrounds the role of academic freedom in supporting not only scholarly inquiry, but also broader forms of social engagement and collective agency. Participants are invited to consider how academic freedom can be understood as a shared responsibility and an evolving practice, rather than a static or purely individual entitlement. Possible Topics• Academic freedom and democratic institutions • Legislative and policy challenges to higher education • The classroom as a space of risk, dialogue, and dissent • Student voice, participation, and vulnerability • Pedagogies of disagreement and difficult conversations • Academic labor, precarity, and speech constraints • Institutional governance and autonomy • Rebuilding trust in higher education • Academic freedom in digital and platformed environments • Global perspectives on academic freedom

items.fullDescription: Thomas Mann, who would have been 100 in 2025, left readers a number of critical challenges. For one, the coded way in which Mann writes about his most dangerous subjects (homosexuality; knowledge of German guilt) still can fool by a credulous reader, meanwhile his essentializing treatment of race, gender, ethnicity, and class is shockingly unabashed. Then, there is the problem of Mann's reversal of political attitudes as the Nazis drove him-the loyalest of native sons-from Germany. As a young reactionary during the First World War, Mann wrote Reflection of an Unpolitical Man, showing such sympathy with the German politics of expansion and aggression in it that he famously considers whether perhaps the sinking of the Lusitania was a reasonable price to pay for the special German destiny. In the aftermath of World War II, under pressure from his children, Mann publicly denounced the Third Reich. Today, he is widely celebrated as a champion of democracy and opponent of Nazism on the global stage. This panel invites responses to the many contradictions of Mann's personality, which permeate his novels, diaries, and essays with remarkable consistency. Responses need not attempt to resolve these discrepancies, but rather interpret them. How do you relate to Mann as an authorial figure? Are there works by him you find troubling but love anyway? This is an opportunity to practice approaching an author's style with sympathetic care and moral scrutiny in equal part. In addition to Mann's queerness and biraciality (both of which he handled with discomfiting ambivalence), topics mights include such Thomas Mann favorites as music, medicine, language, philosophy, and even cinematography. Comparisons with other authors, artists, and theorists also welcome.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS / COLLEGE ENGLISH ASSOCIATION ANNUAL CONFERENCE APRIL 1-3, 2027 / ST LOUIS, MO SUBMISSION SITE IS OPEN: https://www.conftool.pro/cea2027 DEADLINE: 11/01/2026 For its 2027 annual conference,the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. we also encourage proposals on GENERAL TOPICS, including AMERICAN, BRITISH, AND WORLD LITERATURES. DON'T KNOW CEA? YOU SHOULD! In December 1938, a group of young academics attending the MLA convention in New York took on the biggest name in their field-the MLA. They chose to forge a new path by organizing into the College English Association and offering a voice to "the college English teachers of America." Their aim was to upend the scholar-teacher dynamic by recognizing teaching as paramount. Today, more than eight decades later, the CEA continues in that same spirit. At our core, we strive to meet these goals through two venues: our Annual CEA Conference and our journal, The CEA Critic. With over 400 active members and a collection of regional affiliates, the CEA welcomes teacher-scholars at all levels-from graduate students to emeritus faculty-who share our belief that teaching is central to who we are and what we do. CEA WELCOMES GRADUATE STUDENTS As always, the CEA extends a special invite to students pursuing a graduate degree, not only to attend the conference but to submit their presentations to the CEA Outstanding Graduate Student Paper competition. The award carries a grand prize of $250 and publication of the winning essay in the CEA's flagship journal, THE CEA CRITIC. NEW FOR 2027:UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. LEARN MORE: https://cea-web.org/cea-2027-%2F-st-louis

items.excerpt: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literatur...
items.fullDescription: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literature as a major field of inquiry, discussions of literary circulation have often privileged routes that pass through metropolitan centers, emphasizing translation into dominant European languages, global publishing networks, and institutions located in the Global North. Yet literary works have long traveled through alternative circuits that connect regions of the Global South directly, producing histories of exchange that challenge center-periphery models of cultural transmission. This seminar invites papers that examine literary relationships among Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, SWANA, Oceania, and other locations within the Global South. Such relationships may emerge through translation, political solidarity, migration, anti-colonial movements, publishing networks, educational institutions, shared aesthetic projects, or indirect forms of influence. They may also involve moments in which Northern institutions, languages, or markets facilitate, mediate, redirect, or constrain South-South encounters, raising questions about whether these exchanges can ever be understood as entirely autonomous. Rather than treating the Global South as a unified category, the seminar seeks to explore its internal heterogeneity, asymmetries of power, and competing visions of solidarity. How do texts travel between Southern contexts? What historical, linguistic, and political conditions make these encounters possible? What role do translators, publishers, periodicals, archives, and digital media play in creating or sustaining South-South literary networks? How might these circulations reshape concepts such as influence, comparison, translation, reception, or worldliness? We especially welcome papers that interrogate the implications of South-South literary exchange for the study of World Literature itself. If literary circulation is not exclusively organized through Northern centers, what alternative maps of World Literature become visible? Can South-South networks offer different ways of imagining literary value, canon formation, and global comparison? By foregrounding overlooked routes of circulation and exchange, this seminar aims to reconsider how World Literature is conceptualized and to illuminate the multiple worlds through which literature moves. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: South-South translation; comparative studies across the Global South; Cold War and Non-Aligned literary networks; postcolonial and decolonial approaches; migration and diaspora; publishing and periodical cultures; digital literary circulation; transregional modernisms; indigenous and vernacular exchanges; reception studies; archives of literary solidarity; and new theoretical approaches to World Literature.

items.fullDescription: REMINDER: SEPTEMBER 22 SUBMISSION DEADLINE American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. items.title: Beyond Hegemony: Masculinities in World and Comparative Literature
items.excerpt: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. Particular attention may be given to how gender intersects with race, class, migration, coloniality, religion, ecology, technology, and cultural memory in shaping collective identities and practices of empowerment. Situated within the broader concerns of World Literature and Comparative Literature, this session seeks to foster dialogue across regions, languages, and traditions while investigating how masculinities participate in the creation-or disruption-of empowered communities. We welcome papers addressing, but not limited to: Comparative constructions of masculinity across world literatures Masculinity and migration, diaspora, or displacement Literary representations of fatherhood, mentorship, and communal responsibility Masculinities in Global South literatures Masculinity and environmental or ecological communities Masculinity, memory, and post-conflict reconstruction Queer and non-hegemonic masculinities in world literature Masculinity and cultural resistance under authoritarian regimes Masculinity, religion, and collective belonging Masculinity and affect in contemporary global fiction

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. Indexing Information for Prospective Authors IGI Global Scientific Publishing meets the criteria for inclusion in major indexing services such as Scopus; however, it is important to note that all indexing decisions are made independently by these services. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. items.fullDescription: What is the real difference between speaking with nature and speaking for it? Is eco-centric thought a universally shared ideology, or does it develop in reaction to historical, philosophical, and socio-cultural contexts? In what way do the fundamental principles of Indian ecology vary from prevailing Western structures? These essential inquiries delineate the parameters of Ramachandra Guha’s Speaking with Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism (2024), which effectively contests the notion that environmentalism is a unidirectional phenomenon dictated by Western influence. This view posits that the rest of the world, particularly the Global South, lacks eco-conscious awareness because it is ‘too poor to be green’.

items.fullDescription: Popular Culture Association (PCA): Health, Humanities, and Popular Culture 2027 Conference, Boston, USA, March 24-27 2027 CFP DEADLINE FOR ABSTRACTS 31ST OCTOBER 2026 Travel Grant Applications due 15th November The mission of the Popular Culture Association is to promote the appreciation and study of popular culture, as well as to advance rigorous, interdisciplinary research that illuminates the complexity, significance, and impact of popular culture across time and around the globe. We welcome and amplify voices from diverse backgrounds, disciplines, and perspectives by creating spaces-both physical and virtual-for scholars, educators, creators, and enthusiasts to connect, share ideas, and engage in meaningful dialogue about popular culture. The Health, Humanities, and Popular Culture Area is excited to receive proposals for the 2027 Popular Culture and American Culture Association Conference in Boston, USA, March 24-27 2027. Proposal topics should fall within the realm of how health is represented in popular culture through the humanities lens (art, books, comics, journalism and news, cinema, music, theatre, television, etc…). We are interested in receiving papers linked to various related Health issues: drugs or narcotics and popular fiction; vaccinations and popular culture; mental health care and the humanities; and clinical care and the arts. For the 2027 conference we are particularly interested again in examining relationships between health and sustainability/biodiversity/climate change in media and popular culture. The WHO (2023) argued that: "Research shows that 3.6 billion people already live in areas highly susceptible to climate change. Between 2030 and 2050, climate change is expected to cause approximately 250 000 additional deaths per year, from undernutrition, malaria, diarrhoea and heat stress alone. The direct damage costs to health (excluding costs in health-determining sectors such as agriculture and water and sanitation) is estimated to be between US$ 2-4 billion per year by 2030. Areas with weak health infrastructure - mostly in developing countries - will be the least able to cope without assistance to prepare and respond. Reducing emissions of greenhouse gases through better transport, food and energy use choices can result in very large gains for health, particularly through reduced air pollution". (WHO, 2023: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/climate-change-and-health) We therefore invite papers that discuss the key role of communications and media in representing the sustainability/biodiversity/climate change threat demonstrating ways in which its significance are presented or, alternatively, ways in which denial are discussed in popular cultural forms. What are the likely ways in which communications can shape our understanding of this important economic, political and social issue? Proposals should be 250-300 words and exhibit a clear connection between health and popular culture. Submission from current paid members will be accepted through the PCA website. Deadline is 31st October 2026. https://sites.google.com/view/2026pcaconference/call-for-papers

items.fullDescription: Anurag Kashyap, as an Indian film director, is to be identified as one who found himself in the crosshairs of transforming social-relations in post-liberalisation urban India and that of fast changing reception of Bollywood cinema in the wake of globalization. While Kashyap, incidentally, first tasted success in 1998, for the script to Ram Gopal Varma's 'Satya', it has to be noted that the trajectory of his acknowledgement as an auteur-director has neither been consistent nor the most traditional in the strictest sense of reception. Therefore, productions, such as 'Paanch' (2000), 'No Smoking' (2007), or even for that matter 'Gulaal' (2009) received very little attention, only to be declared to be of immense 'cult' value a decade or so later. His filmic oeuvre, often considered to be a part of 'Hat-Ke films' (Biswas, 2019), 'Non-Bollywood cinema' (M. Madhava Prasad, 2013), or even 'Mumbai Middlebrow" (Devasundram, 2016); wherein, the self-consciousness of being 'global' in terms of consumption of 'World Cinema' and producing 'Bollywood' films intertwine with each other, thereby creating a disruption to the narrative flow of films by interrogating the pre-Economic Liberalisation grand récit of nation, family and gender. This self-consciousness could be identified, as a possible reformulation of the binaries of 'Global' and 'Bollywood' to replace that of the 'national' and the 'modern'. With his involvement in the Anurag Kashyap Films (2005-present) and Phantom Studios (Formerly Phantom Films, 2010-2018), Anurag Kashyap began to be hailed as one of the sincerest and well-respected 'auteurs' of neoliberal Bollywood, wherein his films have not only remained a permanent fixture in foreign film festival circuits, and has promoted newer directors such as Vikramaditya Motwane, Bejoy Nambiar, Neeraj Ghaywan and debuts of 'bankable' actors such as Vicky Kaushal. Having been an outsider himself within the Bollywood social habitus, Kashyap's meteoric yet inconsistent rise from the margins to the centerfold of Bollywood, where in the global flows of corporate capital meet the self-conscious cinematic of the internationally respected auteur, augments the neoliberal mode of cinematic consumption and its marketability in the best possible way. The proposal for this volume has already been peer reviewed once by a publisher of international acclaim. Based on the recommendations of the same, we are presently, ONLY AND EXCLUSIVELY looking for papers on the following topics/films: · Anurag Kashyap's OTT productions (ex. Sacred Games, Nishaanchi, Bad Cop and other minor ventures. We are looking for atleast one dedicated contribution on Sacred Games) · "Paanch" (2003) · "Kennedy" (2023) · Gender Politics vis-à-vis formation of women characters/ feminine agency in his films. (excluding Gulaal and Gangs of Wasseypur, for which we already have enough contributions) · Global reception of Anurag Kashyap's filmography through film festival circuits and international circulation. PLEASE NOTE THAT WE ALREADY HAVE ENOUGH PAPERS ON GULAAL AND GANGS OF WASSEYPUR, LIKEWISE WE WOULD NOT BE ABLE TO ENTERNTAIN ANY NEW CONTRIBUTIONS ON THEM. We have as of yet garnered interest from an academic publisher on international repute. This cfp is thus in keeping with the initial peer review responses received on the proposal. This volume will be edited by Dr. Devapriya Sanyal (Assistant Professor, Department of English, St. Joseph's University) and Rajarshi Roy (Assistant Professor, Department of English, Vivekananda Satavarshiki Mahavidyalaya). Please email your proposals of around 250--300 words to ak1anthology@gmail.com by 30th October, 2026. Subsequent decision would be communicated on a rolling basis. Prospective contributors will be expected to submit their full chapters of (approximately) 6,000-7000 words including endnotes (referenced in Chicago style) by 15th November , 2026. Please note that while we encourage contributions from all social cultural dispensations, we are ideally looking for contributors who presently have completed and received their doctoral degrees. Devapriya Sanyal is Assistant Professor in School of Communication and media Studies, St. Joseph's University, Bangalore where she teaches film studies, and literature and researches on Film, Gender Studies, Urban Studies and Environmental Humanities. She is the author of several books on film and gender such as Failed Masculinities: The Men in Satyajit Ray's Films (Edinburgh University Press), Gendered Modernity and Indian Cinema: The Women in Satyajit Ray's Films (Routledge, UK), Salman Khan: The Man, The Actor, The Legend (Bloomsbury, India) and Through the Eyes of a Cinematographer: The Biography of Soumendu Roy(Harper Collins).Her latest books on post-independence Hindi film directors titled Bollywood and the First Decade of Independence: Seven Directors in Search of a Nation was published by Routledge UK in July 2025 and about the woman film director Aparna Sen titled Aparna Sen: A Life in Cinema was published by Rupa in August 2025. Her writings have appeared in national and international journals. She has degrees in English and Film Studies from Lady Brabourne College and JNU. Dr. Rajarshi Roy serves as an Assistant Professor at the Department of English, Vivekananda Satavarshiki Mahavidyalaya, Jhargram. He has been awarded a doctorate for his thesis titled 'The 'faithful' Republic and its representations in Indian literary and public discourses: A Study of the changing natures of secularism in post-Independence India', which is prersently under a monograph contract with Springer Nature. He is also one of the editors of the "Green Tagore" series under contract to be published from Peter Lang. He has in the past, been a recipient of the UGC-RUSA 2.0 fellowship to translate Prasanta Kumar Paul's 'Rabijibani' to English from Bangla. He also serves as an Editor (Consulting), Persons with Special Needs and Rehabilitation Management: Issues in Cultural Diversity and Wellbeing, Jadavpur University.

items.fullDescription: Neurodivergent Studies - Popular Culture Association 2027 "Neurodivergent just means a brain that diverges." - Kassiane Asasumasu, Radical Neurodivergence Speaking Neurodivergent Studies at the PCA offers a chance for scholars to have conversations about how neurodivergent approaches to popular culture, fandom, academia, and our own experiences can shape the way we approach the world. Neurodivergent Studies promotes a very open approach to the subject, following in the footsteps of Kassiane Asasumasu, who is credited with coining the term "neurodivergent." Kassiane specifically notes that neurodivergent "is not another damn tool of exclusion. It is specifically a tool of inclusion. If you don't want to be associated with Those People, then YOU are the one who needs another word. Neurodivergent is for all of us" (sherlocksflataffect). Following Asasamasu's leadership, Neurodivergent Studies invites papers on the following topics: o Neurodivergence in popular media o Neurodivergence and/or madness o Neurodivergence and/or disability o Neurodivergence and self/diagnosis o Neurodivergence and the social disability model o Neurodivergence and eugenics o Neurodivergence and intersectionality o Neurodivergence and race/racism o Neurodivergence and gender identity o Neuroqueer theory o Neurodivergent pedagogy o Neurodivergence in the academy o Neurodivergent activism o Neurodivergent community For the Boston 2027 conference, the PCA is running the theme "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." ND Studies provides a wealth of ways to approach this topic, including focuses on questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. Neurodivergent Studies welcomes paper proposals, roundtable proposals, or cross-listed panels with other PCA areas. Submissions are due October 31. We look forward to seeing you in Boston!

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers (submission deadline October 31, 2026) Fairy Tales Area, American Popular Culture Association Annual Conference, 2027 Boston, MA, March 24-27, 2027 The Fairy Tales Area of the Popular Culture Association invites proposals for individual papers, panels, and roundtables for the 2027 annual conference in Boston, MA, March 24-27. We welcome submissions on all aspects of fairy tales, wonder tales, folk narratives, and their afterlives in literature, film, television, digital media, visual culture, performance, education, gaming, and popular culture more broadly. Papers may address oral tradition, literary fairy tales, folklore collections, adaptations, retellings, reception, translation, theory, pedagogy, gender, race, class, disability, nationalism, childhood, religion, ecology, material culture, or transnational circulation. For the 2027 conference, the Fairy Tales Area is especially interested in submissions related to two featured topics: 1. Adaptation of Fairy Tales This topic invites papers on fairy-tale adaptation across historical periods, genres, and media. Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: • contemporary retellings of fairy tales in fiction, film, television, theater, comics, games, and digital media; • fairy-tale villains, monsters, anti-heroines, and sympathetic retellings of traditionally negative figures; • identity, reflection, self-authorship, trauma, agency, and transformation in fairy-tale adaptation; • adaptation as cultural critique, remediation, commercialization, or popular mythology; • fairy-tale motifs across national, linguistic, and media boundaries. 2. Vladimir Propp's Historical Roots of the Wondertale. Marking the publication of the first English translation of Vladimir Propp's Historical Roots of the Wondertale (Indiana University Press, 2025), the Fairy Tales Area invites papers that revisit this major work and consider its continuing relevance for fairy-tale studies, folklore, narratology, adaptation studies, etc. Topics include but are not limited to: • Propp's Historical Roots of the Wondertale in relation to ritual, initiation, kinship, magic, social transformation, and other social and cultural contexts; • uses of Historical Roots of the Wondertale for analyzing particular tales, tale types, motifs, characters, spaces, objects, or narrative functions; • applications of Propp's work to contemporary fairy-tale retellings, fantasy, film, television, animation, gaming, digital storytelling, and other forms of popular culture; • the relevance of Historical Roots of the Wondertale for studying adaptation or recontextualization of older wonder-tale in modern media; • the place of national wonder tales in international fairy-tale scholarship, including issues of translation, circulation, reception, and comparison; • theoretical and methodological reassessments of Propp's work, including comparisons between Morphology of the Folktale and Historical Roots of the Wondertale, Propp's place in structuralism, narratology, folklore studies, anthropology, literary studies, and popular culture analysis, or the strengths and limitations of his method. Submissions on other fairy-tale topics are also welcome. Additional possible topics include: • Afanasiev, the Grimms, Perrault, Basile, Andersen, and other collectors or authors; • oral tradition and literary fairy tales; • fairy tales in film, television, animation, and streaming media; • fairy tales, gender, and sexuality; • fairy tales and religion, ritual, myth, or magic; • fairy tales and pedagogy; • fairy tales in translation; • fairy tales, horror, fantasy, and speculative fiction; • fairy-tale spaces, objects, bodies, animals, and transformations. Besides the scholarly analyses of fairy tales, we may consider creative and artistic projects that engage with fairy-tale traditions, themes, narratives, and their contemporary reinterpretations. Please submit an abstract of approximately 250 words by October 31, 2026. Panel proposals should include a title and brief description of the panel, along with abstracts and bios for each participant. Scholars at all career stages, including graduate and undergraduate students, independent scholars, and international scholars, are welcome. For questions about the Fairy Tales Area, please contact Dr. Olena Leipnik, Fairy Tales Area Chair, PCA, at soc_ovl@shsu.edu

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Dime Novels and Juvenile Series Books, PCA 2027 The PCA Dime Novels and Juvenile Series Books Area is accepting proposals for presentations at the next PCA/ACA annual conference, to be held in Boston, MA from March 24-27, 2027. See the PCA website for more information on the conference and submission guidelines. The area has two distinct but related areas of interest: juvenile series books of all types and eras, including 20th-century publications like those of the Stratemeyer Syndicate and its imitators (Nancy Drew, Hardy Boys, Tom Swift, etc.), as well as more recent and ongoing series (Harry Potter, Twilight, Choose Your Own Adventure, etc.); and the series books' precursors: early popular publications for mass audiences of all ages (dime novels, nickel weeklies, story papers, etc.). Papers addressing either or both of these areas will be considered. Papers may cover (but are not limited to) any aspect of the following topics: authors, publishers, major characters, themes, readership, bibliography or research methods, social commentary, early or noteworthy genre forms, print culture, special collections, and representations of gender, race, class, sexuality, etc. Something new this year: the larger conference has a theme! The 2027 PCA conference theme is "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." Presenters in Dime Novels and Juvenile Series Books are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. However, area presenters might consider engaging with some of the following themes: Adaptations and retellings of dime novels (reboots of Nick Carter for radio and spy paperbacks; silent films and serials, like Frank Merriwell at Yale (1903), The Adventures of Frank Merriwell (1936), or Deadwood Dick (1940); film adaptations of Laura Jean Libbey stories, including A Poor Girl's Romance (1927), When Love Grows Cold (1925), and In a Moment of Temptation (1928); UPN's Legend series; and series fiction (e. g., the many book variations of Nancy Drew over the decades, the Hardy Boys/Nancy Drew Mysteries television show, the Tom Swift and Linda Craig Mystery Hour , the CW network shows of Nancy Drew and Tom Swift , the numerous film versions of Nancy Drew ). Revolutionary themes in any of the above - for example, are there dime novels that take place during the American or French Revolutions ( The Liberty Boys of '76 )? What is the purpose of setting the story in that time period? What do these dime novels and series books have to say about revolutions more generally, and revolutions in the time that they were published? Dime novels and series books that explore technological revolutions or feature the exploits of inventors, like Frank Read and Tom Swift. Fanfiction, transformative works, participatory culture, audience reception, and cultural memory. This could include series books that were based upon real people, such as the Annette Funicello Mysteries that were a five-book series, or the Janet Lennon books. It could include audience reception captured in film magazines or newspaper reviews. Participants do not need to be academics or professional writers; undergraduate submissions are welcome but require sponsorship by a faculty advisor, as per PCA policy. All participants are requested to submit a 250-word abstract with title. First-time participants with this division are encouraged to submit a 1-2 page proposal, including a bibliography, along with the abstract. Email communication is welcomed from potential members desiring feedback on a proposal topic prior to making a formal submission. Early submission is strongly encouraged. Submissions opened August 1, 2026 and are due by October 31, 2026. In order to submit an abstract, you must have an active PCA membership. Please send all inquiries to: Matt Short University of Northern Illinois mshort@niu.edu Emily Hamilton-Honey SUNY Canton emilyhamiltonhoney@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies Southwest Popular / American Culture Association (SWPACA) 48th Annual Conference, February 17-20, 2027 Marriott Albuquerque Albuquerque, New Mexico https://swpaca.org Proposal submission deadline: October 31, 2026 Proposals for papers and panels are now being accepted for the 48th annual SWPACA conference. One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. The Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies area invites paper proposals on topics related to Taylor Swift and/or Swifties from multiple vantage points. Since her debut in 2006, Taylor Swift has become a fixture of popular culture. Her career has been marked by incredible record-breaking highs and infamous tabloid-fodder lows. Known for her sharp lyrics, her evolving cross-genre musical styles, and her dedicated, creative fanbase (the Swifties), Swift's influence has been noted within music, fashion, economics, politics, and other cultural spheres of power. As an interdisciplinary area, we invite papers from multiple perspectives and disciplines. Topics might include, but are not limited to: • Critical interpretations of Swift's lyrics, eras, and/or personas • Considerations of Taylor Swift and politics, feminisms, activism and social justice • Interrogations of Swift and gender, race, class, and other identities/identifications • Analyses of Swift's connections to business, law, psychology, philosophy or other academic disciplines • Arguments about fandom, belonging, relating, creating and other Swiftie concerns • Examples of Taylor Swift's pedagogical relevancy All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Individual proposals for 15-minute papers must include an abstract of approximately 200-500 words and a brief summary of 100 words or less. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. SWPACA offers monetary awards for the best graduate student papers in a variety of categories. Submissions of accepted, full papers are due January 1, 2026. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Taylor Swift and Swiftie Studies area, please contact its Area Chair, Juliette Holder at jholder1@csustan.edu. If you have general questions about the conference, please contact us at support@swpaca.org, and a member of the executive team will get back to you. This will be a fully in-person conference. If you're looking for an online option to present your work, keep an eye out for details about the 2027 SWPACA Summer Salon, a completely virtual conference to take place in June 2027. We look forward to receiving your submissions!

items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). Table of Contents Section 1: Hip-Hop: A Cultural Politic Chapter 1: The Context of Hip-Hop's Roots and Routes in the Early 1970s Chapter 2: Political Movements that Impacted Hip-Hop's Foundation Chapter 3: Hip-Hop's Formal Political Movements like "Rock the Vote" Chapter 4: Hip-Hop and Moral Panic Section 2: Hip-Hop Generating Identity Chapter 5: Hip-Hop and Generational Identity in the "Post-Racial" Era Chapter 6: Obama, Neoliberalism, and Hip-Hop Mainstream Partisan Politics Chapter 7: From "FDT" to Kodak Black: Hip-Hop's Complicated Relationship with Trump Chapter 8: Hip-Hop and the Black Lives Matter Movement Chapter 9: "Alright" and Social Protests Against Police Brutality Section 3: Hip-Hop and the Sports-Industrial Complex Chapter 10: A History of the Relationship Between Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 11: Subculture to Spectacle: The Evolution of Breaking and Olympic Institutionalization Chapter 12: Ice Cube, The Big Three, and Mogul "Activism" Chapter 13: Jay-Z and the Problematics of the Roc Nation-NFL Partnership Section 4: Representing: Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 14: The Politics of Aesthetics: Street Fashion, the Tunnel Walk, and Racialized Pleasure Chapter 15: Generational Agency: From Michael Jordan's Brand to LeBron's "Representation Activism" Chapter 16: The WNBA and Queering Hip-Hop Aesthetics Chapter 17: Hip-Hop Dance as Art and Sport

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers ESOTERICISM, OCCULTISM, AND MAGIC Southwest Popular / American Culture Association (SWPACA) 48th Annual Conference, February 17-20, 2027 Marriott Albuquerque Albuquerque, New Mexico https://swpaca.org Submissions open: September 1, 2026 Proposal submission deadline : October 31, 2026 Proposals for papers and panels are now being accepted for the 48th annual SWPACA conference. One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. Esotericism, Occultism, and Magic invites proposals relating to magical worldviews, practices, and representations, as well as consciousness transformation, the preternatural, the paranormal, hidden meanings, the power of transmutation, and related phenomena. Characteristic methods, beliefs, perspectives, paradigms and techniques include: arcane symbolism, imagery, and aesthetics; unseen forces, spiritual intermediaries, invisible agencies, nonhuman intelligences; synchronous patterns, non-ordinary causation, and anomalous processes. Examples of ideas and systems include Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Sufism, Tantra, Rosicrucianism, Freemasonry, Satanism, witchcraft, sorcery, demonology, astrology, alchemy, yoga, shamanism, parapsychology, as well as psychic and paranormal phenomena, along with beliefs and practices relating to altered states of consciousness, overlapping with the study of mysticism and New Age spirituality, channeling, positive thinking, manifestation, reality shifting, the power of intention, numerology, guardian angels, and Ascended Masters. Esoteric, occult, and magical concepts, beliefs, and practices appear in every culture and civilization; contemporary media and popular culture have embraced them enthusiastically, yet at times have reacted against them. The impact of esotericism, occultism, and magic on genre formation/content and popular cultural perceptions has been profound. Their themes and tropes continue to become increasingly prevalent throughout all media of popular entertainment, including arts, music, literature, film, television, anime, comics and graphic novels, as well as being nearly ubiquitous throughout interactive gaming of all categories and genres. Beyond entertainment media, esoteric, occult, and magical concepts and content appear in online memes and frequently in fashion accessories and aesthetics. Their popularity continues to inspire and provoke a variety of conspiracisms in reaction, along with various fads, trends, moral panics, witch-hunts, witch-crazes, and conspiracy theories. Examples include demonic intelligences in "AI" chatbots, anti-occult-conspiracism in QAnon; adrenochrome confabulations, Illuminati paranoia, bloodline of the Holy Grail beliefs, Satanic Ritual Abuse scandals. All reactions to, and polemics against, esoteric, occult, and magical content in popular culture, as well as projections concerning its presence, are therefore also suitable topics for this Area, as are political, religious, secular, scientific, and scientistic receptions of esotericism, occultism, and magic, along with instrumentalization of related concepts, beliefs, and practices in propaganda, intelligence, and information warfare. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. items.fullDescription: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. In this way, the theory provides the “genus” of which a given film will be a mere “species”. The application of psychoanalytic ideas or Marxist concepts to film would therefore run the risk of depriving the specificity and singularity of the object in favour of the hegemony of the theory. Here, theory would truly live up to its theological vocation (the “theo” in theory refers to God) standing transcendentally above its “object” upon which it would cast its daunting shadow.

items.fullDescription: CFP: Red Reading the Modern Novel Society for Novel Studies (Vancouver, BC; 13-16 May 2027) The organizer seeks papers that apply Red Reading to twentieth- and twenty-first century novels. The literary canon has been expanded brilliantly in the last few decades, and literary critical approaches have shifted away from modes of corrosive critique. There remains however, a dearth of work grounded in Indigenous epistemologies and critical approaches. As an initial response to this gap, this panel seeks to test Red Reading's utility for studies of the novel. Red reading is one of the most exciting new literary critical methods to emerge in this century. First coined in 2010 Jill Carter the term "Red Reading" has been echoed in different frames by Daniel Heath Justice and James H. Cox, worked out in medieval contexts by Brenna Duperon, and consolidated in a 2018 issue of transmotion edited by Scott Andrews. Most simply, it entails bringing Indigenous approaches to bear on non-Indigenous texts, placing "native perspectives at the center of the discussion," asking new questions of the canon, and drawing non-Indigenous texts into Indigenous epistemological, ethical, and historical frameworks (Andrews ii). It goes beyond just adding Indigenous texts to existing studies and courses to advance a new way of reading that shifts the entire frame of reference. Importantly, Red Reading's early adopters have urged non-Indigenous scholars to use it, making it accessible to scholars of all identities. Potential prompts: • How can Indigenous modes of thinking about story and narrative change the critical reception of modern novels? • What would it look like to apply Indigenous epistemologies to canonical texts? • What can we learn about modern novels by taking a Red Reading approach? • How can Red Reading help us both decolonize the curriculum and advance the goals of reconciliation? • What are the stakes of taking a non-Western, Indigenous approach to reading modern novels? • Are the lessons of postcolonialism and decolonial studies applicable here? Or does red reading constitute something different? • Is the modern novel itself amenable to a Red Reading approach, or is it an ideological form that remains alien to Indigenous epistemologies? Queries and 250 word abstracts should be addressed to Stephen Ross at saross@uvic.ca. Deadline for receipt of abstracts is November 1, 2026.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: [Children's and Young Adult Literature] at CEA 2027 Apr. 1-3, 2027 | St. Louis, Missouri The Westin St. Louis Hotel https://cea-web.org/the-conference-hotel The College English Association, a gathering of scholar-teachers in English studies, welcomes proposals for presentations on Children's and Young Adult Literature for our 57th annual conference. Submit your proposal at www.cea-web.org Scholars and teachers of children's and YA lit intimately know the transformative power the right story at the right time can have on an elementary, middle, or high school student. We do not need reminding of how words, and how they are communicated, to young learners have the ability to grow cognitive processes and lead to future generations of lovers of the written word and future torchbearers of the significance of those words coming from the minds of human beings. Coalescing around the conference theme, we consider how the influence of diverse sculpted stories opens the door to deeper discernment across the curriculum. Conference Theme: Gateways For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Tracing its history back to French explorers in the second half of the 18th century, the great city of St. Louis began as a fur trading post named after King Louis IX of France and was established on the ancestral lands of the Osage Nation, Missouria, and Illini Confederacy. Becoming part of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the city famously came to be known as the "Gateway to the West," serving as a launching point for generations of explorers and settlers expanding the frontier. Yet, we must remember that the city also serves as a gateway to its past as part of indigenous lands transformed through its colonial history into a major river port and trading center that fostered migration both outwards and inwards for centuries. Today, St. Louis invites us to reflect on the continued significance of gateways in our 21st-century lives. GENERAL CALL FOR PAPERS GATEWAYS: For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Potential areas of interest: How do gateways expand literary and cultural spaces but also, as access points, mark out boundaries and limits? Do gateways invite gatekeepers to enable and limit access? Is it possible to imagine gateways without gatekeepers? How can we imagine literary and cultural gateways to foster inter-cultural, cross-cultural, and trans-cultural interactions? How do we envision pedagogical approaches to create gateways for our students to new literary vistas, critical thought, and professional opportunities? How can gateways in both their physical and symbolic significances (like the city of St. Louis and the Gateway Arch) connect the territorial to the cultural, imaginative, and spiritual in literary-critical studies? In what ways can we re-imagine our scholarly and pedagogical work to open up interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary gateways? For CEA 2027, we are especially interested topics related to GATEWAYS in texts, disciplines, people, cultural studies, media, and pedagogy. Consider such topics as the implications of political gateways across time and place, cultural gateways of identity, gateways in the media (including social media) and how they impact society, pedagogical gateways of teaching philosophy and their implementation, or personal gateways through autobiography and memoir. GENERAL TOPICS: The CEA Conference encompasses a wide range of areas, including literary studies, creative writing, rhetoric and composition, technical communication, linguistics, and film. We further encourage proposals in areas about our wider role as academics, including student/instructor accountability and assessment, student advising, academic leadership in departments and programs, and the place of the English department in the university. NEW FOR 2027: UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. For additional information or discussion about this topic and its panels, please contact Peter Elliott at pselliott@anderson.edu.

items.fullDescription: Conference Themes We invite submissions that engage with the ethics of artificial intelligence in both specific and general applications. Topics may include, but are not limited to: Arts & Humanities: AI in creativity, authorship, performance, and cultural identity. Business: Automation, labor ethics, and corporate responsibility. Education: AI in teaching, learning, and research integrity; utilizing AI for student success initiatives and learning accommodations; ethical applications and questions related to AI in scholarly activity; AI in K-12 education. Environmental Impact: AI and sustainability, climate modeling, and AI resource consumption. Healthcare & Medicine: Projection models for patient disease development; treatment individuation; individualized medicine; bias in treatment. Law & Policy: Privacy and data usage; the legitimacy of AI in government. Library & Information Science: AI and the new digital divide; algorithmic bias; AI accuracy, mis- and dis-information. Philosophy: AI as moral agents; AI's effect on human autonomy and decision making; human-AI interfaces and the locus of moral responsibility. Science: AI fabrication of scientific data or references; legitimacy of sources for AI training; drug discovery; intellectual property of data from AI discoveries. Theology: AI in moral theology and bioethics; AI applications in healthcare; theological responses to AI development, including those offered in light of Antiqua et nova (2025) and Magnifica Humanitas (2026). Social Justice & Equity: Accessibility, bias, and discrimination in AI systems. Social Sciences: AI as a research tool for data analysis and methodology; AI systems as social entities and their behavioral impacts; algorithmic bias in social research; AI's effects on human social structures and interactions. items.fullDescription: The erotic is a point of infinite signification, a navel in humanity’s symbolic circuit. However, despite its resistance to formalization, it is always in the process of not being written. As Octavio Paz insists, the erotic is a metaphor indelible to the human. As such, it is unsurprising that the manifestations of the erotic in subjective embodied experience are variable and correspond to equally plural treatments of it across the academic panorama. This diverse archive is bound by certain distinguishable threads, in terms of the potentiality of the erotic, its singular relation to language, and to the sphere of sexuality.

items.fullDescription: In January 2026, murals of faceless female silhouettes in yoga poses were scratched around the genital area in the Indian city of Gwalior. The figures depicted no identifiable women; they were attacked anyway. In 2024, sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes of Taylor Swift circulated widely online, demonstrating a very different but related form of image violation. Across a scratched public wall and a fabricated digital image, the same question emerges: what happens when an image of a woman becomes the surface upon which sexualisation, humiliation or punishment is performed? This special issue asks where, if anywhere, a woman’s image can be assumed to be safe.

items.location: Sibiu · Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu
items.excerpt: Travelling Cultural Heritage Circulation and Digital Afterlives Call for Papers Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference 4th edition Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Romania December 10-11, 2026 Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, as part of the FORTHEM Alliance, invites scholars, researchers, and practitioners to submit proposals for the 4th edition...
items.fullDescription: Travelling Cultural Heritage Circulation and Digital Afterlives Call for Papers Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference 4th edition Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Romania December 10-11, 2026 Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, as part of the FORTHEM Alliance, invites scholars, researchers, and practitioners to submit proposals for the 4th edition of the Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference, dedicated to exploring cultural heritage as a dynamic process of circulation across cultural, geographical, institutional, and historical boundaries. The 2026 edition focuses on Travelling Cultural Heritage (TCH): an approach that understands heritage not as a fixed repository, but as a process through which cultural forms, practices, ideas, and meanings move, encounter different contexts, and are transformed along the way. Drawing on Edward Said's "travelling theory", Mieke Bal's "travelling concepts", and scholarship on cultural circulation, TCH shifts attention from mobile objects to the processes through which heritage is transmitted, adapted, appropriated, reinterpreted, and re-signified. Heritage travels through migration, exchange, conquest, education, trade, tourism, collecting, translation, transmedial transfer, and institutional networks. Migrants adapt cultural practices acquired abroad to their home contexts; travelling elites import fashions, recipes, and other cultural products; artistic styles acquire regional forms as they circulate; and networks of institutions, scholars, dealers, and historical circumstances determine how artefacts enter major collections. Such movements involve adaptation and transformation, but also appropriation, exclusion, and unequal centre-periphery relations. Circulation may allow heritage to acquire new meanings, but it may also entail loss. The large-scale purchase, digitisation, and destruction of books for AI training suggests a future in which physical heritage disappears while its digital avatars survive-an extreme form of travel across media and material states, combining virtual preservation with material destruction. More optimistically, AI, data science, interoperable infrastructures, and spatial visualisation can trace cultural circulation, compare contexts, and recover seemingly lost artefacts, including previously unreadable ancient manuscripts. We welcome contributions that engage with Travelling Cultural Heritage from disciplinary and interdisciplinary perspectives, including cultural and heritage studies, anthropology, archaeology, sociology, history, linguistics and literary studies, political science, art history, architecture, digital humanities, economics, media studies, religious studies, drama, film, the performing arts, museum studies, memory studies, and food studies. Contributors are invited to submit abstracts on, but not limited to, the following themes: Travelling Cultural Heritage: theories, concepts, and methodologies; Cultural circulation, transmission, adaptation, and re-signification; Heritage: migration, displacement, and diaspora; Museums, collections, objects, routes, networks, intermediaries, and infrastructures of cultural circulation; The movement of architectural forms, artistic practices, rituals, and cultural traditions; Colonial, postcolonial, and decolonial circulations of cultural heritage; Digital heritage, digital infrastructures, AI, platforms and computational approaches to cultural circulation; Heritage in translation: what changes when cultural forms travel between languages and the production of new heritage meanings Local content, foreign forms: adaptation and naturalisation across literatures; World Cultural Heritage: comparative approaches to heritage beyond national frameworks; Archaeological evidence for mobility, exchange, and cultural contacts; Memory and heritage: overlappings and differences; Case studies of cultural forms, practices, objects, ideas, or meanings that have travelled across contexts. Submission Guidelines Please submit an abstract of 250-300 words, along with a short biographical note (max. 100 words), to Ovio Olaru (ovio.olaru@ulbsibiu.ro) and Daniela Stanciu-P?sc?ri?a (daniela.stanciu@ulbsibiu.ro) by Nov. 15, 2026. The organisers' decision regarding submissions will be communicated by Nov. 20. For effectiveness, please include "Cultural Heritage Lab conference submission" in the subject line of your email. The conference will be held in English, German, and French, and will take place exclusively on-site. We look forward to your contributions! Kind regards, The organisers

items.location: · PopMeC Association for US Popular Culture Studies

The format will be specific to this session, different from a regular panel: presentations must...
items.fullDescription: Consuming US Popular Culture: Media Aesthetics, Ethics and Literacy Virtual Conference | 27-28 November 2026 POSTGRAD SESSION CALL: The conference will integrate a session dedicated to postgrad student presenters, intended as MA students and early PhD students. The format will be specific to this session, different from a regular panel: presentations must be max. 10min-long, be supported with slides, and the extended Q&A will be oriented toward feedback and suggestions. Students are invited to send a proposal (ca. 200 words long, including title and name) to popmec.media@gmail.com, specifying that it is for the postgrad session. The deadline for this session is November 15. FULL CALL: The consumption of popular culture and media, particularly through platforms and social networks, has become one of the most common leisure time activities worldwide, and US productions are one of the most circulated. Television series, films, videogames, TikTokers, podcasters, memes and other forms of digital culture reach global audiences and shape political identities and cultural imaginaries. Far from being mere entertainment, these texts have consequently become intertwined and virtually inseparable from the daily practices through which individuals get their news input and even their education. The purpose of this year's virtual conference is to open a space for the analysis of the ethical principles (or lack thereof) that seem to guide the construction, circulation and reception of public discourses within the popular culture ecosystem, including both more traditional mediums such as television and comics, but also the products that emerge from generative AI. Popular media content exists as a key source of information in public discourse and influences how we interpret contemporary political issues, how we teach and learn, and even how we exist and behave in society. Although media effects have long been proven to be negotiated rather than direct, the understanding of desirable aesthetics, mindless entertainment and the rhetoric used in political discussions have been hugely impacted by AI generated content. With this cultural media environment in mind, this virtual conference invites explorations of US popular culture through the perspective of media ethics, media literacy and aesthetics. We aim at establishing a space of discussion on the political, educational, ethical and social implications of contemporary media consumption through the analysis of US popular culture. The conference welcomes contributions that tackle the ethical dimensions and societal impact of US popular culture across a wide range of media forms and how they operate within the fragmented and algorithmically curated media ecosystem that we inhabit. We welcome analysis of both mainstream and independent productions, historical and contemporary texts, as well as emerging digital practices. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: × Media ethics and the social responsibilities of producers, platforms and audiences × Media literacy as a framework for analyzing contemporary popular culture × Popular culture as a case study for developing media literacy, ethical reasoning and critical thinking in education × The teaching potential behind popular media texts × Media effects and audience reception of US popular culture × Social media trends, influencers and memes × AI aesthetics in popular media × Polarization, misinformation, conspiracy narratives, and the circulation of disinformation through popular media × (Un)ethical representation of minorities × Political communication, civic engagement, and democratic participation through entertainment media × Representation of political and social problems in US popular culture Deadline for proposals: 1 November 2026 We accept abstract proposals for individual presentations (≈ 250 words), as well as full panels (3 presenters, ≈ 250-word description of the panel plus brief abstracts of all papers). Please, submit your abstract proposal via email at popmec.media@gmail.com as a single attachment (.doc, .docx, .odt) including name, affiliation (if any), and contact email. Official website: https://www.popmec.com/2026-virtual/ Registration fees: REDUCED student / unwaged: 15€ | FULL: 25€ | FREE for PopMeC members with active membership

This international academic event seeks to bring together researchers, academics, artists, educators, and professionals from different disciplines to explore the historical, cultural, social, artistic, scientific, and technological dimensions of healing and well-being. The Congress proposes a dialogue between nineteenth-century traditions and contemporary approaches to health and healing, examining continuities, transformations, exchanges, and tensions across the Hispanic world, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Particular attention will be given to the ways in which literature, art, spirituality, traditional medicine, bodily practices, digital technologies, and community experiences have shaped understandings and practices of healing. Suggested themes include: Genealogies of Healing in Nineteenth-Century Hispanic Culture Representations of Illness in Nineteenth-Century Literature and the Press Art and Healing: Music, Dance, Painting, and Theatre as Therapeutic Practices Dialogues between Allopathic Medicine and Traditional Healing Systems Spirituality, Religion, and Healing Practices Healing through Words: Narratives, Discourse, and Therapeutic Processes Convergences between Bodily Practices (Yoga, Pranayama, Sports) and Holistic Health Healing Traditions in Asia and the Caribbean: Exchanges with the Hispanic World Digital Health, Applications, Platforms, and Well-Being Monitoring Ethical and Clinical Risks of Chatbots and Mental Health Technologies Social Media, Virality, and Their Impact on Emotional Health Attention, Cognition, and Technology Digital Churches, the Spiritual Economy, and New Forms of Religiosity Education and Well-Being Public Health Policies in Digital and Multicultural Environments Interdisciplinarity in Health: Intersections between Art, Science, and Technology Imaginaries of Good and Evil in Processes of Illness and Healing Community Well-Being and Territorial Experiences Researchers interested in participating are invited to submit proposals in accordance with the Congress guidelines. For further information, submission guidelines, and updates, please visit the official Congress website

items.fullDescription: Heidelberg Center for American Studies Annual Interdisciplinary Spring Academy Conference Heidelberg, Germany, April 5-9, 2027 Call for Papers The Heidelberg Center for American Studies (HCA) invites applications for its annual Spring Academy on American Culture, Economics, Geography, History, Literature, Politics, and Religion to be held from April 5-9, 2027. The HCA Spring Academy provides 20 international Ph.D. students with the opportunity to present and thoroughly discuss their ongoing Ph.D. projects. The conference offers a forum for Ph.D. candidates in which they can present their research candidly and receive valuable feedback. We encourage applications that range broadly across the arts, humanities, and social sciences and pursue an interdisciplinary approach. Participants can present thesis projects on any subject relating to the study of the United States of America. Possible topics include American identity, issues of ethnicity, gender, transatlantic relations, U.S. domestic and foreign policy, economics, and various aspects of American religion, geography, history, literature, law, musicology, and culture. We also welcome proposals focused on the North American continent at large, i.e. Canada, Central America, and the Caribbean. Participants are requested to prepare a 20-minute presentation of their research project, which will be followed by a 40-minute discussion. The Spring Academy aims to create a congenial atmosphere for scholarly exchange in order to inspire future collaborations and foster networking opportunities for participants. The Heidelberg Center for American Studies is prepared to provide accommodation during the conference week. Thanks to a small travel fund, the Spring Academy can subsidize travel expenses for participants registered and residing in developing and soft-currency countries. Applicants for the travel fund must document the necessity for financial aid and explain how they plan to cover any potentially remaining expenses. Additionally, a letter of recommendation from their doctoral advisor is required.
