items.fullDescription: CFP: Queer Mediterranean - Sex, Gender, and Social Change April 1-3, 2027, Smith College (Northampton, MA) Queer Mediterranean: Sex, Gender, and Social Change is a conference that brings together scholars, artists, and thinkers to explore queer cultures across the Mediterranean from a transhistorical and transnational perspective, with particular attention to the experiences, voices, and cultural productions of women. The conference aims to explore how queer subjects have navigated, resisted, or reimagined structures of power and belonging across the Mediterranean. What does it mean to think the Mediterranean queerly? What new frameworks, methods, or archives emerge from this approach? While centering women's experiences, we remain fully open to contributions that explore queer life in all its forms. Queer Mediterranean explores what becomes visible when we shift the center of queer theory away from Anglophone frameworks. How do Mediterranean histories complicate dominant narratives of queer identity and liberation? How do Mediterranean perspectives challenge or expand existing models of queer community, kinship, and belonging? What do transnational approaches to queerness reveal about the relationship between queerness, language, and translation? The conference will take place April 1-3, 2027 at Smith College. Hotel accommodations will be provided for all accepted panelists. --- We invite proposals for papers that highlight the richness and diversity of queer experiences across time and place. We welcome scholarly work from across the humanities, social sciences, and arts and are particularly interested in interdisciplinary and transnational perspectives. Topics might include (but are not limited to): Queer histories, archives and memory Queer kinship, family, and belonging Queer migration and diaspora Language, translation, and queer expression Queer literature, film, and visual cultures Queer bodies & embodiment Queer geographies and spaces Queer ecologies and the more-than-human Mediterranean Queer labor and economies Queer tourism and Mediterranean imaginaries Colonialism, postcolonialism, and queerness Queer art and creative practice as resistance Queer temporality and futurity Teaching the queer Mediterranean Abstracts (250-300 words) should be sent through the following google form by November 15, 2026. We will notify accepted panelists by December 15, 2026. Contact: Adrián Gras-Velázquez (agrasvelazquez@smith.edu) Gianna Albaum (galbaum@smith.edu)

items.title: (Tentative) Conjure and Obeah Women: Revisiting African American and African Caribbean Literature
items.excerpt: Every culture possesses a set of religious practices that remain unique to it. It is the role of religious custodians to ensure the survival of such practices and preserve them for future generations. Dragged out of their land, uprooted by force, and tied up in chains, the first enslaved Africans landed at the shores of the Atlantic coast during the perio...
items.fullDescription: Every culture possesses a set of religious practices that remain unique to it. It is the role of religious custodians to ensure the survival of such practices and preserve them for future generations. Dragged out of their land, uprooted by force, and tied up in chains, the first enslaved Africans landed at the shores of the Atlantic coast during the period of seventeenth to nineteenth century. Most men and women that were captured and enslaved were predominantly from West Africa. According to Leslie Alexander, they brought with them cultural practices, labor systems as well as spiritual knowledge that was born in their homeland. It is for this reason that African American history finds its origins in pre colonial West Africa. A crucial aspect of West African tradition was that of conjure practices embedded in religions such as Yoruba, Bakongo, and Igbo belief systems. Shortly after arriving on American soil and obtaining access to the English language, enslaved Africans began to exercise conjure practices. In amalgamation with European folk magic and biblical tradition the practice came to be known as Hoodoo or rootwork with conjure women being at the center of it. Conjure women would often perform hexing, folk healing, and divination for other members of the community. Similarly, its sibling tradition, Obeah, found its roots predominantly in the former British colonies of the Caribbean. During the era of slavery, conjure and obeah women were midwives, healers, spiritual protectors, as well as justice seekers. Enslaved and post emancipation Obeah and conjure women were regarded as healers of the community. Obeah practice, in particular, gave women means of bodily agency with the help of herbal contraception as well as abortion that colonial biopolitics sought to control. The term Obeah is referred to and spelled variously as Obiya, Obia, or Obi. It denotes channeling of supernatural forces, spell casting practices, and healing traditions that remain deeply rooted in African and African diasporic religions. In fact, the word "Obia" in Igbo means a doctor or healer. While both of these practices center the figure of a community healer, the slaveholding as well as colonial authorities suppressed and demonised conjure and obeah women. For this reason, conjure and obeah women would often hide behind Christian symbolism, thereby evoking a sense of respect in the enslaved people who viewed them as sacred figures and fear in white slave owners who perceived them as dangerous witches. The proposed book will examine the tradition and evolution of conjure and obeah women within the African American as well as Caribbean context. The proposed book will cover the following sub themes: Obeah/Conjure women and Healing Obeah/Conjure women and Resistance Obeah/Conjure women and Myths Obeah/Conjure women and Culture Obeah/Conjure women and Diasporic Spirituality Obeah/Conjure women and Black Feminism Obeah/Conjure women and Racial Identity Obeah/Conjure women and Folk Traditions The proposed book invites original and unpublished chapters on the above mentioned themes. However, the proposed list is only suggestive in nature rather than exhaustive. Additionally, the proposed book will be submitted to Brill for consideration. Important Deadline: The last date for submission of abstracts is 22nd November 2026. Please read the following submission guidelines carefully before submitting your abstract: Submission Format: Authors must submit an abstract of 200-250 words. A brief bio-note of approximately 100 words must be included. Abstract, bio-note, and keywords must be compiled in a single Microsoft Word document (.doc/.docx). The document should be emailed to: africanliterarystudies15@gmail.com Authors are required to include 3-5 keywords along with the abstract. Detailed guidelines regarding formatting and submission of full-length papers will be shared with shortlisted contributors. For any query or abstract submission, contact africanliterarystudies15@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: When, in September 2026, a post declaring the actress Katrina Kaif "finished" following her return to public life after childbirth accumulated lakhs of views and comments, the disproportion between judgement and object became, itself, the more legible text. A comparable structure recurred that same year for the South Korean singer Jennie, whose performances at Mad Cool Festival and Lollapalooza Chicago drew, alongside widespread acclaim, a coordinated wave of "netizen" commentary deriding her "leaner frame" — two women, two national contexts, two entirely unrelated bodily "failures" (one insufficiently youthful, the other insufficiently substantial), and yet an identical infrastructure of mass, public, collectively affirmed judgement.

items.title: Destination Management and Mobility Justice for Sustainable Human and More-than-human Futures: Approaching Florence (and Destinations Beyond) in Motio
items.excerpt: In this interdisciplinary conference, we seek to examine critical issues in the field of global Destination Management and Tourism Mobilities in pursuit of means, modes and practices to promote a greater Mobility Justice within, between, and beyond destinations (Sheller 2018; 2024). Situated within the Florentine context, this conference offers fertile gr...
items.fullDescription: In this interdisciplinary conference, we seek to examine critical issues in the field of global Destination Management and Tourism Mobilities in pursuit of means, modes and practices to promote a greater Mobility Justice within, between, and beyond destinations (Sheller 2018; 2024). Situated within the Florentine context, this conference offers fertile ground for cross-pollination between Florence and other destinations concerned with how Destination Managers and Destination Management Organizations (DMOs) can be pivotal actors, agencies, and organizations committed to a more just, sustainable, and responsible mobile world. As the politics of mobility play out in real time through the bodies and streets, we see local, national and transnational governance struggle to keep pace with the impacts and drivers of climate change, urbanization, and migration. All the while we watch as mass tourism and overtourism thread impacts through micro, meso, and macro scales. Simultaneously, migrants, refugees, asylum seekers, undocumented, stateless, and trafficked persons experience increasing pressures and injustices through the same forces that support the most mobility privileged in global tourist flows. In this entangled web of mobility regimes and infrastructures, it is important to examine where travel and tourism have historically been a cultural force for promoting peace and dialogue, as much as examining where conflict, friction, and tensions have arisen from them. Destinations offer an opportunity to analyze and intervene at specific sites of human migrations and mobilities, and what in hopes of more just tourism mobilities in destinations across the world. Florence is no stranger to conflicts over tourism mobilities and tensions within its unique identity as a site of global patrimony. As a destination caught in the crosshairs of its rich past and an uncertain future in this age of polycrisis, conflicting representations and identities intersect, diverge, and weave a complex social fabric. Destination Management offers a targeted lens through which to interrogate the relation between global travel, tourism and mobility justice in Florence and beyond. As a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Florence represents a rich cultural tourism destination that is increasingly impacted by increasingly global flows and circulations of people, objects, artifacts, information, resources and capital. It has resulted in intersecting crises of housing displacement and homelessness, food insecurity, growing civil protest, increasing environmental resource and climatic constraints, uneven distribution of tourist fluxes between major and minor cultural sites, and loss of local goodwill in response to the immobilities created by tourism. This conference seeks to bring to light the complexities of questions of justice in a hypermobile world. How does one respect cultural heritage while local peoples and cultures suffer across so many dimensions, often deprived of their cultural rights, unable to access their own heritage sites? How do we support human and more-than-human futures, adaptable and responsive to environmental constraints, changes, and challenges? Many questions arise that require interdisciplinary perspectives. We invite papers to contribute to the emerging field of Destination Management, focusing on the intersections of issues in social, cultural, environmental, and mobility justice within the roles and responsibilities of Destination Managers and DMOs (Destination Management Organizations). We welcome a wide range of disciplinary perspectives and methods, including case study analyses, historical or contemporary mobilities, and theoretical contributions that are committed to exploring what Justice means within Destination Management theory and practice. Thematically, we ask contributors to examine how questions of justice can be integrated into interdisciplinary Destination Management scholarship that contend with the domains of travel and tourism. Submissions can include both normative and empirical research broadly relevant to informing questions of Justice and Mobilities, and can broadly range from social sciences, STEM, humanities, and arts fields, and present either contemporary or historical perspectives. We aim to explore where various areas of justice can be connected to the objectives of Destination Management research as a growing interdisciplinary field. We encourage scholars and practitioners to investigate the applicability of distributive, deliberative, procedural, restorative, and epistemic justice in the framework of their presented contributions. We are interested in case studies which either (A) center their analyses on Florence, Italy (or the region of Tuscany) in order to seek translatable and transversal solutions for other destinations, or (B) center on global destinations beyond that bring critical insight into the issues facing Florence. We are seeking to find "common ground" amongst the examined problem spaces that exist across destinations to build a growing literature concerned with promoting Mobility Justice within Destination Management. Theoretical contributions should include insight or practical application to transversal issues across Florence and other destinations. SUBMISSION GUIDELINES: We ask for 300-word abstracts, submitted with a separate cover page that includes title, name, affiliation, and a short bio of the author(s) of a maximum of 300 words, which can be submitted to dstm@gonzaga.edu by November 25th, 2026. The conference will be held from March 11th to 12th at Gonzaga in Florence, a school of Gonzaga University based in the historic center of the city of Florence. It will be open to the public, by registration. There will be no registration fee to attend the conference. As our inaugural conference, we are unable to offer travel funds at this time. Topical Areas: 1. Mobility Justice (motility, capabilities approach, migration, transport, space, accessibility, flows) a. Migration, refugees, stateless persons, human trafficking and modern day slavery b. Critical Disability Studies & mobility infrastructures for travel & tourism industries c. The Right to the City, labour, and yransportation equity d. Mobility, technological transformation, and electrification e. Climate Mobility Justice and immigration/refugee crises 2. Social Justice (intersectionality, human rights, kinopolitics distributive justice, reparation, processual justice) a. Indigenous Rights and Land Consent b. Human rights Abuses in the travel and tourism industry c. Intercultural exchange for responsible, sustainable, and peace tourism d. Reparative justice, public policy, media, and communications e. Critical Disability Studies and transport justice 3. Cultural Justice: (heritage studies, restoration and repatriation, cultural property, political ecology) a. Art, antiquities, museum studies, and decolonization b. Cultural heritage, human rights, and access to culture c. Cultural property trafficking, return and restitution, reclamation, and reparations d. Museum security, contemporary eco-vandalism and protest movements e. Conflicts in historiography of heritage and Post-conflict reconstruction 4. Environmental Justice (environmental racism, geoengineering, pollution and carbon, biodiversity and reparations, More-than-human ethics): a. National parks, seascapes, urban green space, and depavement movements b. Plastic pollution, chemical colonialism, exposomics, and water protectors c. Protected habitats, ecotourism and politics of spared or shared land d. Agriculture, food Justice, "The Commons", land sovereignty, and eco-activism e. Botanical gardens, zoos, "beasts of burden", and more-than-human mobility Conference Organizers: Denise Regina Percequillo Hossom Gonzaga University Alesia Koush Gonzaga University UNESCO Chair - University of Siena

items.fullDescription: At many universities, learning communities foster connectedness and belonging among students. Learning communities are typically composed of cohorts of students taking aligned first-year classes, but they take many other forms as well. At their best, they promote the perspective that learning is a collective activity in which knowledge is constructed through relationships with peers, professors, and communities, bringing together diverse voices and interdisciplinary perspectives. They provide a welcoming environment that eases the transition to college and provides a foundation for a peer network of academic support (Schreiber & Valle, 2013).

items.title: Beyond Climate Crisis: Multidisciplinary Perspectives on Human-Environment Relationships in a Warming World
items.excerpt: Beyond Climate Crisis: Multidisciplinary Perspectives on Human-Environment Relationships in a Warming World Loreto College Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences, published by Loreto College (Autonomous), Kolkata The full paper should be emailed to lcjhss@loretocollege.in (with a cc to loretocollegemdj@gmail.com) Last Date of submission of paper: Novem...
items.fullDescription: Beyond Climate Crisis: Multidisciplinary Perspectives on Human-Environment Relationships in a Warming World Loreto College Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences, published by Loreto College (Autonomous), Kolkata The full paper should be emailed to lcjhss@loretocollege.in (with a cc to loretocollegemdj@gmail.com) Last Date of submission of paper: November 30, 2025. Climate change and the ensuing climate crisis is no longer the subject matter of scientific definitions and policy solutions. It is an unfolding truth sensed through the lived experiences of human communities. The villages and cities we inhabit, the migrations forced out of them, the economies we develop, the inequalities they reinstate, the institutions that govern us, the systems that fail us, the grief and anxieties that plague our minds, the resilience with which we survive ecological crises, the stories we tell, the language we tell them in, the education we deliver in classrooms, the screens that captivate our young generation, and the shared future that we all move towards; are tied by at least one single distinct thread of commonality - the crisis of a changing climate, a warming world. It is imperative to recognize that the degradation of our planet profoundly reshapes both human consciousness and the stability of our institutions. The intensifying weight of ecological distress, combined with feelings of accountability toward future generations and the trauma of environmental catastrophes, underscores the psychological tension between personal helplessness and the power of communal action. The theme of this edition of LCJHSS however, seeks to go beyond this crisis associated with a warming climate. Rather than treating climate change as a matter of purely scientific discourse demanding only policy interventions, this issue takes it out of the domain of the expert to the everyday life of the people who are affected. Without undermining the science of climate change and climate policy, the current issue tries to move beyond alarming predictions toward a more layered engagement with how societies across the globe are interpreting, resisting, adapting to, and being reshaped by a warming world. The issue is organized around several interlocking threads of inquiry allowing major social science disciplines to interpret climate crisis and human-environment interrelationships through the sub-themes enumerated below. These threads are interwoven through their explicit commitment to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals on health and well-being (SDG 3), clean water (SDG 6), sustainable cities (SDG 11), responsible consumption (SDG 12), climate action (SDG 13), life below water (SDG 14), and life on land (SDG 15). These goals are not merely abstract targets but are lived, contested, and deeply human concerns. By integrating geographical assessments with the study of literature, and merging historical inquiry with insights from psychology, economics, and film, this publication seeks to create a shared space for intellectual exchange. We invite researchers, professionals, and social advocates to move beyond traditional academic boundaries and look past the despair of end-of-the-world scenarios. Our goal is to define constructive routes toward communal resilience, fairness, and the restoration of our fragile world. We invite papers on the following subthemes for the third volume of Loreto College Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences: Narratives of Loss, Resilience, and Ecological Grief Water, Forests, and Landscapes in Literary Imagination Food, Agriculture, and Environmental Narratives in Literature Animal Studies, Multispecies Narratives, and the More-than-Human World Climate Finance, ESG and Sustainable Economic Governance Climate Resilience, Livelihoods and Development in the Global South Integrating climate change, biodiversity, and sustainability into school and higher education curricula. Eco-Pedagogy and Nature-Based Learning Addressing environmental inequality through gender-responsive, disability-inclusive, and socially just educational practices. The Anthropocene in world literature Ecological crises in literary history The language and rhetorics of climate change Eco-Cinema and Environmental Storytelling. Documentary Films as Tools for Climate Advocacy. Disaster Cinema and Climatic Resilience. Reimagining Human-Nature Relationships in Contemporary Cinema. Climate-Induced Migration and Displacement - migration, displacement, resettlement, vulnerability mapping, and adaptation corridors. LULC Change and Landscape/Ecosystem Transformations - deforestation, urbanization, agricultural shifts, contributing to and impacted by climate change. Urban Microclimate - heat islands, green infrastructure, urban planning, and lived experience in warming cities. Spatial Modelling of Environmental Change - satellite-based monitoring, LST mapping, environmental vulnerability and risk modelling. Genealogies of Environmentalism: Non-Western, Indigenous, and counter-hegemonic histories of conservation and eco-centrism. Resilience, Migration, and Collapse -re-evaluations of societal "collapse" versus adaptation strategies during past environmental stress. The history of mono-cropping, deforestation, and land enclosure in shaping global ecological imbalances. The historical tension between communal resource management and private/state property regimes Climate Communication, Environmental Journalism, and Public Engagement for Sustainable Futures Media, Biodiversity, Water, and Coastal Sustainability: Narratives for Ecological Resilience Sustainable Cities and Communities: Urban Sociology Gender Inequality in the Age of Sustainability: Sociology of Gender Environmental Policy and Governance in a Warming World Examining the role of national and international policies, treaties, and governance structures in addressing climate change. Political Economy of Climate Change Analyzing how economic interests, resource distribution, and market mechanisms influence climate policies and environmental justice. Power Dynamics and Environmental Justice Investigating how power relations shape climate vulnerability and access to resources among different social groups and nations. Climate Change and State Sovereignty Exploring tensions between national sovereignty and global climate commitments, including issues of compliance and enforcement. The Role of Civil Society and Political Movements Assessing how activism, social movements, and civil society influence environmental policymaking and climate action. Security and Conflict in a Warming World Studying the links between climate change, resource scarcity, and political instability or conflict. Multilevel Governance and Climate Adaptation Understanding the interactions between local, national, and international political institutions in climate resilience strategies. Climate Policy, Democracy, and Public Participation Evaluating democratic processes, public engagement, and political accountability in climate decision-making. Futures of Climate Politics: Negotiations, Diplomacy, and Geopolitics Analyzing the evolving geopolitics of climate negotiations, including the roles of major powers and emerging economies. Ethics, Responsibility, and Climate Justice- Discussing moral and political responsibilities of states and actors toward vulnerable populations and future generations. Eco-Anxiety, Climate Grief, and Mental Health Disruption Climate Justice, Vulnerability, and Equity (frontline, Indigenous, and low-income populations experience trauma from climate disasters,Place Attachment and Identity Loss, psychological tensions between generations regarding responsibility, guilt, and inherited environmental degradation ) Collective Action, Social Norms, and Agency (How social norms, peer networks, and ideological identities influence eco-conscious choices, Psychology of Activism) Nature Connectedness, Restorative Environments, and Well-Being Climate Resilience (Moving away from hyper-individualism and anthropocentrism toward relational, ecological worldviews, how communities process climate-driven adversity to build stronger social cohesion, adaptive capacity, and shared purpose) CALL FOR PAPERS Papers are invited for the third volume of the online, peer-reviewed, multi-disciplinary annual journal, Loreto College Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences, published by Loreto College (Autonomous), Kolkata (established in 1912). The scope of the journal includes interdisciplinary studies spanning Cultural Studies, Economics, Education, Film Studies, Gender Studies, Geography, History, Human Rights, Language, Literature and Literary Criticism (English and Bangla), Media Studies, Political Science, Psychology and Sociology. About the Journal 1. Each issue is theme-based and articles are invited on the proposed theme from scholars across the world. There is a wide-range of sub-themes in keeping with the multidisciplinary nature of the journal. 2. Each article is submitted for anonymous review by distinguished scholars from relevant fields. 3. The journal publishes articles purely on their academic merit as recommended by the referees. It accepts no submission or publication charges as it is fully funded by Loreto College. 4. The journal has e-ISSN and individual papers/articles will be assigned DOIs. AUTHOR GUIDELINES FOR SUBMISSION Submissions should be original and not previously published elsewhere or submitted for consideration to any other journal. Manuscripts may be rejected without peer review if they do not comply with the instructions for authors. Research papers from Post-graduate students should be co-authored with a faculty member of a college or university. The submission should consist of 4 documents: The Research Paper- a single document consisting of- a) title page - should contain the Title, Name/s of Author/s, Designation and Affiliation, mobile number and e-mail ID. b) abstract - should be within 300 words. The abstract should provide a summary of the paper indicating the scope, range and theoretical perspectives. It should contain the title of the paper. It is submitted to different indexing bodies and collections of abstracts. Therefore, it should be written in lucid English keeping the international reader in mind. c) key words - four/five keywords d) full paper - the paper should contain the entire article including the title. No borders or decorations are required. All charts, tables, figures and illustrations should be placed in relevant places in the main body of the paper itself. Authors will be responsible for negotiating permission if and where necessary for reproducing illustrations, etc. Permission should be sought well in time so that there is no delay in publication of the journal. Bio note of the author/s ? Plagiarism Report Author's Declaration - The author must submit a declaration in the format given below stating that the paper submitted is his/her original writing and that it has not been submitted to any other journal or publisher for publication. For papers which are not found suitable for publication, the corresponding author will be informed via email. Format for Author's Declaration I, ------------ hereby declare that this manuscript represents my original work and that all sources used have been appropriately acknowledged. I confirm I have both contributed significantly to the research presented in this paper and agree with the content as submitted. To the best of my knowledge, no conflict of interest exists that could have influenced the research findings. This article has not been submitted to any other journal or publisher for publication. I am aware that if published the copyright of the article would belong to Loreto College, Kolkata. Name: Signature: Designation: Email: Phone number: Date: The full paper should be emailed to lcjhss@loretocollege.in(with a cc to loretocollegemdj@gmail.com) Last Date of submission of paper: November 30, 2025. General Instructions The email containing the paper must include the name of the discipline in the subject line of the email. For papers with more than one author, please indicate the corresponding author clearly on the title page. Length of contributions- Research Articles (2,500-5,500 words including notes and references); Book Reviews (600-1,500 words) The contributions should be submitted in MS Word (Times New Roman, Font size 12) The APA citation style should be used. Please refer to https://apastyle.apa.org/style-grammar-guidelines/references/examples. Not following the correct citation style (APA) may be grounds for rejection. Missing references/citations should be avoided. Authors are advised to insert only those references that have been mentioned in the manuscript. The text (in font size 12) and end notes (in font size 11) should be double-spaced. Do not justify the text or the notes. All quotations should follow the original exactly in respect of spelling, capitalization, italicization, punctuation, etc. Quotations not exceeding 25 words may run on with the text and should be in single inverted commas. Quotations longer than 25 words should be indented 0.5 on both sides without quotation marks. Such block quotations should be in font size 10 and single spaced. Full details are to be provided for other sources such as facsimiles, newspaper articles, interviews, material on microfilm, websites (page title, full URL and date of access), etc. For act, scene and line references to plays, the italicized title should be followed by a comma, act no. in capital roman numerals, stop, scene no. in lower-case roman numerals, stop, line no.(s) in Arabic numerals. Example: Ben Johnson, Volpone, II.ii.10-12. Titles of constituent sections, essays, poems, etc. should be placed within single quotation marks. British spellings are preferred to American alternatives. The copyright of all articles published in the journal will belong to Loreto College, Kolkata. Specific Guidelines for Tables, Artwork and Illustrations ? All tables should be submitted separately (i.e. not within the body of the manuscript) in a single text file. ? Tables should not be in picture format. ? Tables are to be numbered using Arabic numeral 1 only, serially as 1.1, 1.2., 1.3, etc. Tables should not be numbered as 2, 3, and so on. ? Tables should always be cited in text in consecutive numerical order. ? Each table should have a table caption (title) explaining the components of the table. ? Identify any previously published material by giving the original source in the form of a reference at the end of the table caption. Artwork and Illustrations Guidelines 1. Figures (charts, graphs, diagrams, maps, etc.) should be supplied as separate JPEG image files. 2. The image resolution should at least be of 1000 px width. 3. The file should be named by the figure number. 4. All figures are to be numbered using Arabic numerals. 5. Figures should always be cited in text in consecutive numerical order. 6. Figures and figure parts should be denoted by Arabic numeral 1 only, serially as 1.1, 1.2, 1.1.1, 1.2.1 etc. Figures should not be numbered as 2, 3, and so on. 7. Each figure should have a concise caption accurately describing what the figure depicts. Include the captions in a separate text file. 8. Figure captions begin with the term Fig. in bold type, followed by the figure number, also in bold type. 9. No punctuation is to be included after the number, nor is any punctuation to be placed at the end of the caption.

items.excerpt: Call for Papers: Literary Gardens: Cultivation, Movement, and Modernism An International Online Conference | February 12-13, 2027 | Online sponsored by The Elizabeth von Arnim Society in conversation with The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & Gardens in Narratives Stephen and Peter Sachs Museum, Missouri Botanical Garden The Elizabeth von Arnim...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Literary Gardens: Cultivation, Movement, and Modernism An International Online Conference | February 12-13, 2027 | Online sponsored by The Elizabeth von Arnim Society in conversation with The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & Gardens in Narratives Stephen and Peter Sachs Museum, Missouri Botanical Garden The Elizabeth von Arnim Society invites paper proposals for an international online conference on literary gardens, held in conversation with the Missouri Botanical Garden exhibit The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & Gardens in Narratives (Sachs Museum, May 2026-March 2027), curated by Nezka Pfeifer. Inspired by the exhibition's wide-ranging exploration of plants and gardens, this conference will consider gardens as spaces of literary cultivation, movement, and modernity. Gardens are never simply settings: they are imagined spaces, sites of labor and care, refuge and restoration, social and cultural exchange, but also places of exclusion, transgression, and imperialist pilfering. Plants, people, texts, ideas, and botanical knowledge move through them. Gardens can therefore illuminate modernism's preoccupation with mobility, displacement, belonging, transformation, and the relationship between the human and more-than-human worlds. The conference centers on modernism, broadly conceived, including fin-de-siècle precursors and modernism's later extensions and legacies. We are particularly interested in women's garden writing, including that of Elizabeth von Arnim, as well as the ways gardens participate in transnational literary and cultural networks. We welcome work on African American, Caribbean, diasporic, queer, Indigenous, and other perspectives that complicate and expand histories of modernism and the literary garden. We warmly encourage you to share this call with colleagues, graduate students, and independent scholars Keynote Speakers: Nezka Pfiefer, curator of The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & Gardens in Narrativesat the Sachs Museum, Missouri Botanical Garden Karina Jakubowicz, author of Gardens in the work of Virginia Woolf: Nature, Modernity, and the Politics of Space (2026 Edinburgh UP) We welcome proposals on subjects including, but not limited to: Cultivation and Modernist Cultures Elizabeth von Arnim and the literary garden Fin-de-siècle garden writing, including Oscar Wilde and Gertrude Jekyll Women, gardens, and modernist cultural production, including Elizabeth von Arnim, Virginia Woolf, Katherine Mansfield, H.D., and Edith Wharton Gardens as spaces of artistic, literary, and intellectual exchange War, Healing, and Remembrance The healing garden: refuge, restoration, remembrance, and renewal Peace gardens and gardens of reconciliation in the aftermath of war Gardens, illness, disability, care, and the body Gardens, Labor, Identity, and Space Gardens, labor, class, domestic service, and foodways, including Agnes Smedley and Zora Neale Hurston Gardens, gender, sexuality, queer identity, and the body, including Vita Sackville-West and Beverley Nichols Gardens as spaces of hospitality, community, and cultural production Comparative and translation studies of literary gardens Gardens, archives, botanical history, museums, and exhibitions Movement, Migration, and Belonging Plants, people, texts, ideas, and botanical knowledge in circulation Gardens, migration, diaspora, exile, and the imagination of home Cultivation, transplantation, naturalization, displacement, and belonging Gardens, empire, colonialism, and postcolonialism African American modernism and the garden, including the Harlem Renaissance, Anne Spencer, and Black cultural networks Caribbean and transatlantic modernisms, including Alejo Carpentier and Claude McKay Global and transnational modernisms, including Mário de Andrade Gardens, Plants, and Modernist Form Gardens and modernist poetry, including T. S. Eliot and Sara Teasdale Gardens in fiction, including gothic, speculative, fantasy, mystery, and children's literature Gardens, plants, and the more-than-human: monstrous flora, sentient gardens, and speculative botany Writing in the garden: composition, retreat, and creative practice Ecocriticism, plant studies, and botanical modernisms Gardens, books, illustration, and modernist print culture Submission Guidelines Please submit an abstract of approximately 250 words for a 20-minute paper, or for a full panel (3-4 papers) 250 words per speaker. Include a short biographical note (100 words) for each speaker. Submit through our submission form: forms.gle/pqbJjueSge3pAFoL9 by November 30, 2026. Notifications of acceptance will be sent by mid-December 2026. The conference will be held online on February 12-13, 2027. Sessions will be scheduled with an international audience in mind; a detailed program, including access information, will follow upon acceptance. About the Elizabeth von Arnim Society The Elizabeth von Arnim Society is dedicated to fostering scholarly work on Elizabeth von Arnim (1866-1941) and to helping scholars from around the world exchange ideas about her life and writing. For more information, visit elizabethvonarnimsociety.org. Questions? Questions about the submission form or the conference more generally can be directed to Noreen O'Connor at noreen.oconnor@mac.com.

items.fullDescription: Overview | South Mediterranean University, Tunisia Hybrid Format: In-person and Online Participation The SMU Conference on AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms will take place at South Mediterranean University, Tunisia. This research oriented event brings together scholars, educators, instructional designers, and researchers to explore evidence-based pedagogical innovation in technology-mediated and AI-enhanced learning environments. This conference provides an international platform to present academic research, foster interdisciplinary dialogue, and advance collaboration on the future of teaching and learning in the AI era. The 2027 SMU Conference, themed "AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms," examines how AI and emerging educational technologies reshape instructional design, classroom engagement, assessment, and learning ecosystems. Key focus areas include measurable learning outcomes, ethical and inclusive AI integration, pedagogical quality assurance, and student competency development in hybrid and digital environments. We invite researchers, practitioners, instructional designers, and graduate students worldwide to submit original research, empirical studies, and case studies on innovative pedagogy, AI-enhanced instruction, learning analytics, engagement strategies, and inclusive practices.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Volume 37, Issue 1 & 2 (2027) Dear Colleagues, Litera: Journal of Language, Literature and Culture Studies - Dil, Edebiyat ve Kültür Ara?t?rmalar? Dergisi, the official publication of the Department of Western Languages and Literatures at Istanbul University, invites submissions for its 2026 issues (Volume 36, Issues 1 & 2). An open-access, peer-reviewed, and multilingual journal published twice a year (June & December), Litera is indexed in ELSEVIER SCOPUS, Web of Science ESCI, MLA International Bibliography, DOAJ (Directory of Open Access Journals), ERIH PLUS, EBSCO Communication Source, EBSCO Central & Eastern European Academic Source, Gale Cengage and Ulrichsweb. While our core focus remains on literary studies, linguistics, and cultural studies, we welcome interdisciplinary approaches that combine literary and linguistic analysis with insights from cultural theory and media studies-provided they maintain a clear relevance to our aim and scope We welcome original research articles that engage with current debates and critical issues in the study of Western (American, English, French, Belgian, German, Swiss, Austrian, Italian, Spanish, Latin American and Modern Greek) languages, literatures, and cultures. In particular, we encourage contributions that reflect cutting-edge scholarship in areas such as, but not limited to: · Contemporary literary theory · Disability Studies · Human-Animal Studies · Posthumanism and critical posthumanities · Ecofeminism and ecocriticism · Ecosemiotics and Ecolinguistics · Discourse Studies · Intersectional and decolonial approaches · Digital humanities and media theory · Film Studies · Medieval Studies · Posthuman Communication Studies · Gender studies · Narrative and identity in contemporary fiction · Transnationalism and migration literature · Crete studies Submission Windows: · Issue 1 (June 2027): November 1-30, 2026 · Issue 2 (December 2027): May 1-31, 2027 Submission Guidelines: Manuscripts must be original, unpublished, and not under review elsewhere. items.title: Star Wars at 50: Forces, Forms, Legacies

items.fullDescription: 2027 marks the 50th anniversary of the film now generally known as Episode IV: A New Hope , the first instalment in the hugely successful Star Wars franchise created by George Lucas. As beloved as it is divisive, Star Wars now straddles multiple decades and generations while proliferating across narrative media (novels, comics, games, animation, TV). It provides a series of compelling case studies in the relationship between creativity and commerce, from the foundation of Lucasfilm during the New Hollywood period to the 21st century Disney-era, and it has developed via a complex interplay between cutting-edge technological innovation, nostalgia, and mythmaking.

items.fullDescription: Over the past three decades, fan studies have developed sophisticated accounts of participatory culture, collective intelligence, affective engagement, and transformative practices (Jenkins 2006; Booth 2015; Hills 2017). At the same time, scholarship has increasingly addressed the investigative dimensions of audience participation. Mittell’s concept of “forensic fandom” (2009), for example, highlights practices of close reading, clue collection, speculation, and collaborative interpretation in response to complex narrative worlds. Fans thus become active investigators who uncover hidden meanings, solve mysteries, and assemble fragmented information across media texts. More recently, such investigative practices have expanded beyond fictional worlds.

items.title: The Four Horsemen of the Bropocalypse: Power and Culture Under a Tech Oligarchy
items.location: Bloomington, Indiana, United States · Indiana University
items.excerpt: CALL FOR PROPOSALS The Four Horsemen of the Bropocalypse: Power and Culture Under a Tech Oligarchy March 25-27, Bloomington, IN, Indiana University Bloomington The first quarter of the twenty-first century has been organized, to a degree that bears sustained scholarly attention, by a small cohort of men whose private fortunes rival the budgets of nation-s...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PROPOSALS The Four Horsemen of the Bropocalypse: Power and Culture Under a Tech Oligarchy March 25-27, Bloomington, IN, Indiana University Bloomington The first quarter of the twenty-first century has been organized, to a degree that bears sustained scholarly attention, by a small cohort of men whose private fortunes rival the budgets of nation-states, whose platforms mediate the social and epistemic lives of billions, and whose biographical idiosyncrasies have become structural features of global infrastructure. Steve Jobs furnished the template; Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, and Peter Thiel have inherited and transformed it. This conference takes the tech founder seriously as a political, economic, aesthetic, and theological problem, and as an object adequate to humanistic inquiry. The planning committee invites proposals for individual papers, pre-constituted panels, and roundtables across three streams - the Horsemen, their Mounts, their Kingdom. Comparative, transnational, and historically minded approaches are particularly welcome. Stream One: The Horsemen The Four Leaders of the Bropocalypse The figures themselves - as biographies, personae, cultural texts, and authors and products of their own myths. Questions to consider: How do we read the founder's letter, the keynote, the congressional testimony, the tweet? What work does biography do for the founder, and the founder for biography? How are their bodies stylized, optimized, and displayed? What is the cultural work of the turtleneck, the gilet, the cage match, the longevity protocol, the pronatalist announcement? How do spatial fantasies, such as the bunker, the compound, the rocket, the company town, relate to longer traditions of utopia, sovereignty, and flight? Where do the horsemen sit in longer histories of capital - Hearst, Ford, Hughes, Rockefeller - and alongside transnational counterparts? Stream Two: The Mounts Technological Foundations of the Bropocalypse The material, infrastructural, and epistemic conditions that made these figures possible and that they have, in turn, reshaped - the technologies the horsemen ride. Work drawing on media theory, STS, infrastructure studies, and the political economy of computing is especially welcome. Questions to consider: How do recommender systems and engagement metrics constitute attention as a political resource? How should we read the fulfillment center, the algorithmically managed workplace, the gig contract? What happens to the worker when the workplace is built to render the worker illegible? What are the climatic, hydrological, and territorial costs of the immaterial satellite constellations, undersea cables, data centers? What models of mind, language, and sociality are inscribed in the chatbot, the agent, the avatar? How do these systems reshape pedagogy, friendship, intimacy, grief, work? Stream Three: The Kingdom Institutional Context of the Bropocalypse The regulatory, financial, philanthropic, cultural, and political ecology that has enabled, legitimated, and at moments resisted the formation under analysis - the terrain across which the horsemen ride. Questions to consider: What is the worldview of contemporary venture capital, and how is it produced and reproduced through the manifesto, the LP letter, the founder-mode essay? How has the research university - its endowments, donors, dropout mythologies - both produced and been remade by the founders it educated and abandoned? What does it mean that the largest funders of causes such as global health, climate response, and basic research are now the personal foundations of living billionaires? How should we understand the migration of significant fractions of tech capital toward the American right, and the ideological projects - network state, accelerationism, neoreaction - that have traveled with it? What can scholarship learn from counter-formations such as Wikipedia, the Fediverse, platform cooperativism, the union drive, and open protocol? Submission Guidelines Proposals for individual papers (20 minutes) should consist of an abstract of no more than 350 words and a brief bio (100 words). Panel and roundtable proposals should include a 250-word rationale alongside individual abstracts. Please indicate the stream; the committee reserves the right to reassign. Submissions at https://forms.gle/uf5jwkNVWDBHbVcq9 by December 1, 2026. Decisions by January 30, 2027. Please direct any questions to bropocalypse2027@gmail.com. Edward Dallis-Comentale, Erin Kelley, Amber Bowes, Robert Metaxatos Indiana University Bloomington

Through the lens of ecocriticism, this collection will analyze how narratives represent, question, and critique e...
items.fullDescription: Myths have long shaped how humans understand and interact with the natural world. This edited collection examines how contemporary science fiction streaming television draws on mythology to explore humanity's relationship with the environment. Through the lens of ecocriticism, this collection will analyze how narratives represent, question, and critique environmental responsibility, ecological interconnectedness, and humanity's impact on Earth, or other worlds. Since 2008, John Perlich and David Whitt have co-edited three books on comparative mythology: Sith, Slayers, Stargates, and Cyborgs (2008), Millennial Mythmaking (2010), and Myth in the Modern World(2014). This fourth collection, which will be published by McFarland & Company, seeks to bring together scholars and cultural critics from a variety of fields (e.g., mythology, environmental studies, media, cultural studies, literature, political science, anthropology, sociology, communication studies) to examine contemporary and original science fiction television on streaming services. Streaming platforms have emerged as premier destinations for ambitious, avant-garde, commercially successful, and critically acclaimed science fiction. The following is a partial list of original science fiction shows on various streaming platforms: · Amazon Prime Video: Fallout, The Expanse, The Rig, Outer Range · Apple TV+: Foundation, Silo, For All Mankind, Pluribus, Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, Dark Matter, Star City, Invasion · Disney+: Star Wars (The Mandalorian, Andor, Ahsoka, Visions, Skeleton Crew), Marvel (Loki, Moon Knight) · HBO Max: The Last of Us, Dune: Prophecy, Raised by Wolves, Station Eleven · Hulu: Paradise, Solar Opposites · Netflix: Stranger Things, Black Mirror, Love, Death + Robots, 3 Body Problem, Sweet Tooth, Dark, The Eternaut, The Rain, The Silent Sea · Peacock: The Ark, Twisted Metal · Paramount+: Halo, Star Trek (Discovery, Lower Decks, Picard, Starfleet Academy, Strange New Worlds) The rich and varied programming on these streaming services provides a myriad of opportunities to examine contemporary science fiction television in terms of mythology and the environment. Some potential topics include: · Creation myths and the making of new worlds and ecosystems · The Hero's Journey and the environment · The impact of science and technology on the environment · Monsters, aliens and others environmental threats · Climate change, apocalyptic and dystopian worlds · Ecofeminism and mythology · Environmental activism · Allusions to mythic protectors (e.g., Gaia, Artemis, Demeter, Nüwa, Sedna, etc.) Please submit a proposal by December 1, 2026. Proposals should include: - a 500-1000 word abstract - brief author bio - contact information Chapters will be limited to 5000-6000 words and must follow APA style guidelines (7th edition). Send questions and proposals to both co-editors. John Perlich Bemidji State University john.perlich@bemidjistate.edu David Whitt Nebraska Wesleyan University dfw@nebrwesleyan.edu

items.excerpt: CALL FOR PAPERS The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media Edited by ?rem Atasoy and Habib Tekin The edited volume The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media seeks to explore representations and conceptualizations of artificial, technologically modified, replicated, and human-like bodies from...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media Edited by ?rem Atasoy and Habib Tekin The edited volume The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media seeks to explore representations and conceptualizations of artificial, technologically modified, replicated, and human-like bodies from interdisciplinary perspectives. Rather than approaching the artificial body merely as a product of technological development, the volume considers it as a cultural and semiotic site through which changing ideas of embodiment, identity, agency, consciousness, corporeality, and human-machine relations are negotiated. Cyborgs, clones, androids, humanoid robots, synthetic beings, technologically augmented humans, and other forms of artificial or hybrid embodiment have long occupied the cultural imagination. Their representations raise fundamental questions concerning the limits of the human: Where does the human body end and the artificial begin? What happens to identity when the body can be modified, replicated, reconstructed, or manufactured? How do artificial bodies challenge established distinctions between subject and object, organism and machine, self and other? And how do literature and media participate in constructing, questioning, or transforming these boundaries? Situated at the intersections of literary studies, media studies, cultural studies, semiotics, philosophy, and posthumanist and transhumanist thought, the volume welcomes both theoretical contributions and analyses of individual or comparative works. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: · cyborgs and hybrid embodiment · clones, replication, and biological identity · humanoids, androids, and human-like artificial beings · artificial bodies and posthuman subjectivity · transhumanism and technological enhancement · human-machine boundaries · embodiment and artificial intelligence · synthetic and technologically constructed bodies · body modification and augmentation · artificial bodies and questions of identity, memory, and consciousness · the body as sign and the semiotics of artificial embodiment · gender, sexuality, and artificial bodies · artificial bodies in science fiction and cyberpunk · utopian and dystopian representations of technologically transformed bodies · virtual, digital, and simulated bodies · avatars and disembodied/re-embodied identities · artificial bodies and questions of agency and autonomy · the uncanny, the monstrous, and the artificial human · ethics and politics of creating, modifying, and replicating bodies · historical transformations in representations of artificial humans Contributions may examine literary texts, films, television series, graphic narratives, video games, digital narratives, or other relevant media and may employ approaches from literary and cultural studies, media and film studies, semiotics, multimodality, narratology, posthumanism, transhumanism, critical theory, gender studies, or related fields. The volume will be published as part of Interdisciplinary Studies on Philology by Maurer Press, an interdisciplinary series bringing philological research into dialogue with contemporary approaches from literary, linguistic, cultural, media, and related fields. Submission Guidelines Abstract length: 300-500 words Include: title, author name, affiliation, ORCID Formatting: Times New Roman, 12 pt, 1.5 line spacing Abstract submission deadline: December 4, 2026 CPC: The CPC for publication in this volume is 150 Euro per chapter. Publisher: Maurer Press, Germany Important Notes Full chapter length, style sheet, and timeline will be communicated upon abstract acceptance. All submissions should be original and not under consideration elsewhere. The editors and publisher reserve the right to make final selections based on peer review and fit with the volume. Please send abstracts and inquiries to: irem.atasoy@istanbul.edu.tr and habib.tekin@marmara.edu.tr

items.fullDescription: Two-day National Conference on Sustainability calls for a dialogue between Indigenous knowledge and contemporary cultural practices. Bringing Indian Knowledge Systems into critical dialogue with humanities academic discourse, this conference aims at exploring literary and cultural responses to ecological uncertainty and technological changes during current times. Drawing on the concerns of rapid technological advancement, ecological health and cultural representations, it looks forward to advancing interdisciplinary approaches grounded in social justice, ethical responsibility, and communal co-existence. Objective: Advancing interdisciplinary research, critical discourse & academic collaboration through indigineous, comparative and transnational perspectives. The conference welcomes scholarly contributions on, but not limited to the following sub-themes: Sustainability and Literature from the Margins Gendered Spaces in Literature and their Impact on Sustainability Crisis, Care, and Continuity: Pandemic Literature, Indian Knowledge Systems, and Sustainability Human-Animal Relations, Indian Knowledge Systems, and the More-than-Human World Artificial Intelligence at the Intersection of Literature and Sustainability Blue Humanities and the Cultural Imagination of Sustainability Environment, Media and Popular Culture Rethinking Physical Education and Sports in Modern Times Cinema, Public Memory and Social Crisis in Contemporary India Indigenous Sustainability, Heritage, and Traditional Ecological Knowledge Eco-Horror, Slow Violence, and the Aftermath of Climate-Induced Migration Alternative ways of Knowing: Indigenous Knowledge Systems in Conversation with Western Frameworks Turning Care into Change: Sustainability through Corporate Social Responsibility Registration fee: Research scholars: INR 2,000 Student/Independent Scholars: INR 1,500 Faculty: INR 2,500

items.title: Comparative Visual Satire: Methodology, Subjectivity and the Global Gaze
items.excerpt: Comparative Visual Satire: Methodology, Subjectivity and the Global Gaze An interdisciplinary workshop on caricature, iconography and the politics of seeing One-day workshop for graduate students at Heidelberg University - March 12, 2027 From novels, essays and plays to cartoons, music, paintings and internet culture, satire has always been society's one...
items.fullDescription: Comparative Visual Satire: Methodology, Subjectivity and the Global Gaze An interdisciplinary workshop on caricature, iconography and the politics of seeing One-day workshop for graduate students at Heidelberg University - March 12, 2027 From novels, essays and plays to cartoons, music, paintings and internet culture, satire has always been society's one of the favourite tools for speaking uncomfortable truths. It travels across borders, opens doors into other cultures and illustrates political and social life. But above all, at its best, it makes us laugh. Yet the tools we use to read and compare satirical images remain largely inherited from Western traditions of iconographic analysis and rarely interrogate their own situatedness. How can visual forms of satire be studied academically? What are the methodological challenges involved in analysing cartoons from other cultures? How does the subject of study relate to the researcher and vice versa? This workshop takes these questions seriously. Bringing together PhD and postdoc scholars at different stages of their researches, the workshop aims to create space for methodological reflection alongside hands-on practice. We are particularly interested in what happens when analytical frameworks developed in one cultural context are applied to visual material produced in another and in building more honest, rigorous approaches to that challenge. As such, we invite researchers working across the fields of visual culture, media studies, art history, literature and cultural studies to join a focused workshop on the methodologies and critical challenges of studying visual satire comparatively and across cultural contexts. Which topics can be discussed Topics discussed in the workshop may include the following ones. Though, these do not constitute a limitation. Other topics and research objects are warmly welcomed! o Comics and caricatures o Satire on the internet o Cartoons (films, programmes and magazines) o Plays o Operas o Paintings and art o Buildings o Iconographic analysis of visual satire o Inter- and transmedia approaches o Comparative and cross-cultural frameworks o Practice-based and visual inquiry methods o Subjectivity and positionality o Race, gender and ethnicity in caricature o Identity frameworks and satirical representation o The Western gaze on non-Western material o Non-Western researcher's Western lens on non-Western material o Decolonising the satirical archive It doesn't matter how old the subject of study is or where in the world it comes from. One thread running through the workshop is the specific set of challenges that arise when Western-trained researchers engage with visual satire produced outside Western traditions. After the workshop, we will have collectively developed a working list of the critical issues and blind spots that this kind of research demands for our further research. Format The workshop deliberately avoids the conventional conference structure of presentations followed by brief questions. Instead, we're planning to use a fishbowl format: a participatory, non-hierarchical setup in which both invited contributors and all attendees engage as equals throughout the day discussing the research material. Each participant is invited to introduce a question, case study, methodological problem or provocation in approximately five minutes. This opening aims to be a starting point instead of a full presentation. What follows is a collective discussion in which everyone contributes from their own perspective, disciplinary background and research experience. Sessions will alternate between discussion and hands-on experimentation. We are convinced that that approach gives participants the opportunity to test ideas with visual material and to see how different analytical approaches produce different readings of the same image. Therefore, we encourage you to bring a sample of your research material with you. The whole workshop will be held in English. Who should attend This workshop is open to anyone whose work touches on visual satire, caricature or illustrated media whether from art history, media studies, cultural studies, postcolonial studies, journalism studies or adjacent fields. We welcome researchers especially at early career stages and PhD students and particularly encourage participation from scholars working on non-Western or underrepresented satirical traditions. Location and time The workshop will take place over one day in Heidelberg on March 12, 2027. The venue will be the Käthe Leichter Forum, Im Neuenheimer Feld 370, 69120 Heidelberg. How to apply We ask anyone interested to submit a brief application to Gamze [gamzealtinyaprak.h@uni-heidelberg.de] and Alexander [alexander.reindl@ori.uni-heidelberg.de] by December 6, 2026. Applications should include: o a short paragraph (150-200 words) describing your research topic and subject; o a brief biography (50-100 words); o a research object/problem you want to discuss in the plenary. We look forward to receiving your applications and will get back to you with our decision by December 21, 2026 with further details. Don't hesitate to contact us if you have any questions regarding the workshop or the application.

items.fullDescription: Arconexiones. Graduate conference of the Spanish Master's students of the Department of Anthropology and Languages at ISU Cartographies, Spaces and Borders: Exploring Limits and Possibilities "Borders are set up to define the places that are safe and unsafe, to distinguish us from them. A border is a dividing line, a narrow strip along a steep edge. A borderland is a vague and undetermined place created by the emotional residue of an unnatural boundary. It is a constant state of transition. The prohibited and forbidden are its inhabitants." -Gloria Anzaldúa "Nothing suggests the feeling of boundless spaces quite like silence" -Gastón Bachelard Virtual Idaho State University Saturday, February 20, 2027 9am-4pm Mountain Time (GMT-7) Keynotes: Dr. Abel Arango Skidmore College Luis Benavides Idaho State University In considering this year's theme, the conference organizers propose an exploration of spaces and borders-both in their physical and conceptual dimensions. Maps, as a starting point, offer us not only a visual version of the world we inhabit but also reflect our perspectives, what we value, and how humans seek to control, separate, and name these spaces. They contain clues regarding political and military history, conflicts, and abuses of power. To take possession of these territories, the Europeans who arrived in the Americas often described these lands in great detail-creating, in effect, maps made of words. For their part, the Indigenous peoples of these lands possess their own ways of understanding their spaces, which are deeply rooted in their cultural values. We see spaces under control, spaces that bear different names depending on the culture or language, spaces that are private, public, or shared-and an endless variety of ways to conceive of them. The work "América Invertida" ("Inverted America")-an ink drawing by the Uruguayan artist Joaquín Torres García-offers an inspiring perspective, presenting the South American continent as viewed from the south. Another significant contemporary map is the "Equal Earth" projection, adopted by the United Nations in September 2026, which provides a more accurate representation of the actual size of the continents. Maps have long been a fixture on the walls and in the textbooks of our schools; they shape the initial concept of the nation for young citizens. We invite you to explore the idea of space in all its forms - beyond both the geographical and the physical - and to enter into the realm of liminality, the transitional states between two places, the boundaries between disciplines or genres, and the marginality of certain groups or individuals. Can one feel, through cultural productions, a sense of belonging - or not belonging - to certain spaces? Do these cultural productions create new spaces for their readers, even though those spaces are fictional? Literary spaces are often reflections of our desires or fears, or our imaginations grappling with oppressive reality as a form of escape. Consider the famous, and sometimes magical, settings of Hispanic literature, such as Macondo, Comala, José Martí's "Our America," Al-Ándalus, or La Mancha. They linger in the mind long after we finish reading, and we continue to explore them. In this sense, for the fourth edition of the Arconexiones conference, we invite graduate and advanced undergraduate students from ISU and other universities to present work in fields such as film, literature, cultural studies, theater, pedagogy, critical theory, social studies, visual arts, music, and performance. We seek submissions that reflect on the concepts of cartographies, spaces, and borders within the context of Peninsular, Latin American, and Latinx cultural production. The goal of this gathering is to analyze how literary narratives, artistic productions, and diverse cultural expressions contribute to the construction or destruction of new borders. Suggested thematic areas include, but are not limited to: Critical cartographies and counter-cartographies: History of cartography; colonial and post-colonial maps; participatory mapping; community and Indigenous mapping; social, queer, and feminist cartographies. Social production of space: Territories, places, and landscapes; contested territories; urban and rural spaces; geographies of memory and extractivism. Borders, boundaries, and contact zones: National, internal, and symbolic borders; border regions; migration, displacement, and mobility; walls, checkpoints, and crossings; hybrid and liminal spaces (e.g. Nepantla). Cultural representations of space: Literature, film, art, and photography; imaginary maps and narratives of territory (e.g., Macondo, Comala, or La Mancha); ekphrastic descriptions of maps in literature; toponymy and soundscapes. Spatial technologies and digital humanities: Geographic Information Systems (GIS); remote sensing; digital cartography; open data; artificial intelligence and surveillance; ethics of geographic data. Construction of national identities and nations: such as Benedict Anderson's concept of "Imagined Communities," nation-building following independence, and also in Doris Sommer's "Foundational Fictions." Spaces, environment, and futures: the climate crisis; watersheds; oceans, and amphibious territories; transboundary spaces and governance; cartographies of the Anthropocene. Innovations in pedagogy and linguistics: Spanglish as a tool for identity; borders and contact zones between languages ??(code-switching, translanguaging); barriers to acquisition and/or learning; new linguistic spaces created on social media and the Internet that challenge geographic boundaries; taking language learning beyond the classroom walls (experiential learning or virtual learning). Interested applicants can submit a 200-250 word abstract of their original research work (or proposal) and with a title. Presentations will be accepted in English or Spanish, lasting 15 minutes (approximately 8 pages double-spaced), with additional time for questions and comments. The deadline for submissions is Monday, December 7th, 2026. For more information, contact us at marinlaufenberg@isu.edu or visit the conference website: https://www.isu.edu/anthropology/student-experience/arconexiones-conferenceconferencia/ Send your proposals using this link before Monday, December 7th, 2026-- https://forms.gle/Jy4SPKbsjDwBQYWc7

items.excerpt: Call for Chapters: One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft For thousands of years, embroidery and embroidered work have been used as a mode of visual storytelling and of documenting national or cultural histories. items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters: One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft For thousands of years, embroidery and embroidered work have been used as a mode of visual storytelling and of documenting national or cultural histories. From the 12000 years-old fiberwork found in the Guitarrero Cave, to twine textile artwork of the Peruvian Norte Chico civilization of 2500 BCE, the thousands of years old Chinese silk thread embroidery, the decorative thread arts of the Indus Valley Civilization of 3000 BCE, the ancient Egyptian needlework of 1300 BCE, the Bayeux Tapestry of Norman conquest, and the thousands of years old embroidery and quilt work of the indigenous communities across the North and South Americas, human civilizations have woven and embroidered their histories and cultures and have archived everything for future generations. Embroidery has also functioned as a powerful trope of resistance narrative and rebellious vision. Marjorie Agosín's iconic book, Tapestries of Hope recounts how Chilean women used embroidery and textile art as tools of resistance and rebellion during Pinochet's dictatorship. More recently, Kirstie McLeod's collaborative project "The Red Dress" brings together the needlework, voices, and stories of 380 individuals from 51 countries. Collectively, their embroidered experiences on a single red dress, across a range of expertise, positions, and languages, testify to human rights concerns around the world. In the context of underprivileged women from the global South, embroidery and needlework have been a source of financial freedom and a platform for women's social bonding and personal expressions. For example, cottage industries in Bangladesh, India, and many other South and East Asian countries have mobilized economically impoverished women into an active workforce and have turned embroidery and needlework into a booming business. In literature and media, embroidered works also provide intense narrative power. Adrienne Rich's "Aunt Jennifer's Tigers" and Rosa del Valle's tablecloth in Isabel Allende's The House of the Spirits, are two such examples. Embroidery has provided a pertinent motif for re-presenting folklore, myth, and collective memory in many countries, such as Bangladesh and India, where women's acts of illustrating folklores, personal loss and pain in quilts or narrating the mythical stories of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata through needlework are an essential part of their national and cultural history. Textile arts, embroidery and needlework function as narrative technologies that initiate individual, social, and political involvement. It invokes memory and provokes individuals to make or break myths regarding nation, narration, gender, identity, and/or human existence in the age of artificial intelligence. Against this extensive backdrop of embroidery as a narrative technology, we invite abstracts for a collection tentatively titled One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft. Tentative topic list for the paper (but is not limited to): Archiving history through embroidery Embroidery as narrative technology Embroidery as a trope of Agency and/or Identity Embroidery as a narrative of political resistance Embroidery as Storytelling Embroidery and human rights or social justice Embroidery and activism Embroidery and/in literature Embroidery and/as cultural identity Embroidery and/as visual narrative Embroidery and ecocriticism Myth, memory, and embroidery Retelling myth and re-presenting identity Women and embroidery Please send us your 150 words abstract with 3 key words and a 50-word bio by December 10, 2026. If accepted, we will request for the completed essay (minimum of 7000 words) by June 30, 2027. The anthology is expected to be published by a university press in the US. Looking forward to receiving your abstract at fayeza.hasanat@ucf.edu , cc farrah.cato@ucf.edu Sincerely, Dr. Fayeza Hasanat and Dr. Farrah Cato English Department University of Central Florida
