items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTER PROPOSAL The Ghost in the Machine Learns to Speak for the Dead: AI, Rhetorical Resurrection, the the Injustice of Synthetic Voice An edited Collection, edited by Shiva Hari Mainaly, PhD, University of Memphis Abstracts due December 15, 2026 The Dead are Speaking. Who Gave Them Their Words? In May 2025, a man killed in a road-rage shooting appeared to address his killer at a sentencing hearing in an Arizona courtroom. His face, his voice, and his words of forgiveness were all generated by AI, scripted by his family, and accepted by the judge. The moment moved some and deeply unsettled others. It also signaled what was to come. Generative AI can now produce convincing speech in the voices of the dead, from grief chatbots that let mourners "talk" with a lost parent to reconstructed testimonies of historical victims and posthumous "final statements" circulated online. A growing digital afterlife industry has turned the voices of the dead into products (Hollanek & Nowaczyk-Basi?ska, 2024; Öhman & Floridi, 2017), while deepfakes threaten the very idea of testimony as evidence (Chesney & Citron, 2019). This collection argues that AI resurrection is not a neutral technical feat. It is a rhetorical act, with speakers, audiences, purposes, and consequences. Rhetoric has long named this move: prosopopoeia, the figure that gives voice to the absent and the dead. What is new is its scale, its realism, and the authority it borrows. Building on the concept of phantom ethos, the fabricated credibility that AI lends to synthetic speech, we ask what happens when a machine speaks as someone who can no longer consent, correct, or refuse. These questions are not evenly distributed. Those most likely to be reanimated are often those already dispossessed of voice by histories of violence, colonialism, and erasure. Scholars have long warned about the ethics of speaking for others (Alcoff, 1991) and asked whether the subaltern can speak at all (Spivak, 1988). In particular, Saidiya Hartman (2008) has shown both the necessity and the danger of imagining lives the archive silenced. Today, such imagining can be automated, sold, and stripped of its care. When synthetic voice fills the archive's silences, it risks a new form of epistemic injustice (Fricker, 2007): the dead are made to testify, but not on their own terms. Since technologies encode the inequalities of their makers (Benjamin, 2019; Noble, 2018), we must ask whose voices are resurrected, whose are distorted, and whose are simply ignored. We invite chapters that offer a distinctly rhetorical intervention into a conversation now dominated by legal and computer science perspectives. We welcome theoretical, historical, critical, empirical, and pedagogical work, and we especially encourage contributions from scholars in the Global South, from Indigenous and minoritized communities, and from early-career researchers and graduate students. Guiding Questions Who holds the authority to speak for the dead, and how is that authority built, borrowed, or faked? What does consent mean for people who cannot give it? Who should decide: families, estates, communities, platforms, or states? How are courts, newsrooms, museums, and platforms using synthetic voice, and what counts as truth or testimony there? Whose voices are resurrected, and whose histories of violence make them especially vulnerable to reanimation? Can synthetic voice ever serve justice, memory, or repair? What would an ethical practice look like? How should we teach students to read, question, and resist synthetic testimony? Possible Topics We are organizing the collection around five clusters. Proposals may address one or several; topics beyond this list are warmly welcome. Part I. Theorizing Resurrected Voice ? Phantom ethos, synthetic credibility, and ethos without a body ? Prosopopoeia, apostrophe, and classical figures of speaking for the absent ? Hauntology, spectrality, and the rhetoric of the digital ghost (Derrida, 1994) ? Voice, timbre, race, and the politics of listening to machines (Eidsheim, 2019) Part II. Synthetic Testimony in Courts, Newsrooms, and Platforms ? AI-generated victim impact statements and deepfaked evidence ? Journalists "interviewing" AI recreations of the dead ? Documentaries, advertising, and cloned voices of deceased public figures ? Platform policies, labeling, and the governance of posthumous speech Part III. Grief, Memory, and the Digital Afterlife Industry ? Griefbots, deadbots, and the commercialization of mourning ? Consent, estates, and data rights after death ? Religious, cultural, and non-Western rituals of speaking with ancestors ? Museums, memorials, and interactive testimony projects Part IV. Voice, Violence, and Erasure: Who Gets Reanimated? ? Resurrecting victims of colonial, racial, and state violence ? Critical fabulation versus algorithmic fabrication in the archive ? Indigenous voices, sovereignty, and data governance ? Endangered languages, Global South speakers, and linguistic justice ? Gender, disability, and the reanimation of marginalized bodies and voices Part V. Pedagogy, Policy, and Resistance ? Teaching students to analyze synthetic media and testimony ? Technical and professional communication guidelines for synthetic voice ? Right of publicity, likeness laws, and AI policy ? Community-led refusal, counter-archives, and design justice approaches Why Contribute? ? Shape a new field. The rhetoric of AI resurrection is still largely unwritten. Your chapter can help define its vocabulary. ? Reach across disciplines. The collection speaks to rhetoric and composition, media studies, AI ethics, law, memory studies, and technical communication. ? Join a global conversation. We are building a volume that is international, interdisciplinary, and attentive to voices too often left out of AI debates. ? Receive thoughtful editorial support. Every accepted chapter will receive developmental feedback and peer review. Submission Guidelines Please send the following in a single Word document or PDF: ? A chapter title and an abstract of 300-500 words, not counting references ? Three to five keywords ? A short list of key references (optional) ? A biography of up to 100 words for each author, with affiliation and email Email submissions to shminaly@memphis.edu with the subject line "CFP: Synthetic Voice Collection - [Your Last Name]." Full chapters of 6,000-8,000 words, including references, will follow APA 7th edition style. Co-authored and interdisciplinary chapters are welcome. Please do not submit work that is published or under review elsewhere. Milestone Date Abstracts due December 15, 2026 Notification of acceptance January 31, 2027 Full chapters due June 30, 2027 Peer review and feedback to authors September 30, 2027 Revised Chapters due December 15, 2027 Final manuscript to publisher Early 2028

items.fullDescription: "Creativity, Resistance and Social Change" International Conference 27-28 February 2027 St Anne's College, University of Oxford & Online organised by London Centre for Interdisciplinary Research Across history and cultures, creativity has played a central role in resisting injustice, challenging dominant narratives and imagining alternative social futures. From storytelling, music and visual art to literature, performance, digital media and everyday creative practices, acts of creation often emerge in response to exclusion, oppression or crisis. Creativity can unite communities, give voice to marginalised experiences and sustain collective struggles for dignity, justice and transformation. This conference invites interdisciplinary reflections on how creative practices function as forms of resistance and catalysts for social change. We welcome contributions that explore creativity both as an expressive response to power and as an active force shaping social, political and cultural transformations. Possible themes Include (but are not limited to): Creativity as resistance and dissent Storytelling, memory and counter-narratives Oral traditions, folklore and cultural transmission Literature, poetry and narrative activism Music, performance and protest cultures Visual arts, street art and public space Digital creativity, social media and online resistance Youth cultures, creativity and social movements Gender, sexuality and creative resistance Indigenous, postcolonial and decolonial creative practices Creativity, migration, displacement and belonging Art, trauma, healing and social repair Creative economies, labour and social justice Education, pedagogy and creativity for social change We welcome submissions from across the humanities and social sciences, including but not limited to literature, anthropology, sociology, history, cultural studies, media and communication, psychology, education, political science and the arts. Proposals may take the form of: Individual papers Panel or roundtable proposals Practice-based or creative presentations Community-engaged or participatory research Paper proposals up to 250 words and a brief biographical note should be sent by 15 December 2026 to: creative-voices@lcir.co.uk.

items.fullDescription: Social Inclusion, peer-reviewed journal indexed in the Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus, welcomes new and exciting research papers for its upcoming issue "Inclusive Diversity in European Education: From Policy Frameworks to Classroom Practices," edited by Roberto Baelo Álvarez, Alessandro Bergamaschi, and Anna Elia. Submission of Abstracts: 1-15 December 2026 Submission of Full Papers: 15-30 April 2027 Publication of the Issue: June/December 2027 About the issue: Contemporary European societies are characterised by an unprecedented degree of diversity (linguistic, cultural, ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic), challenging the foundations of traditional educational systems. The concept of superdiversity, which moves beyond binary majority-minority frameworks to account for the complex intersectionality of identities and trajectories, reflects the lived reality of classrooms, schools, and universities across the continent. However, educational policies and pedagogical practices have often lagged behind this transformation, generating tensions between normative aspirations for inclusion and the structural conditions shaping everyday educational contexts. This thematic issue brings together interdisciplinary scholarship examining how educational systems across Europe and beyond are responding, or failing to respond, to the challenges and opportunities posed by diversity. Drawing on sociology, educational science, political science, and intercultural studies, the issue addresses four interconnected dimensions: the normative and policy frameworks governing diversity in education; the social implications of superdiversity for educational communities, particularly the tension between demands for equality and differentiation in everyday school situations; the pedagogical approaches, teacher education strategies, and curricular innovations aimed at fostering inclusive learning environments; and the perspectives of key actors, including students, educators, institutions, and civil society. Finally, the issue aims to critically examine whether inclusion can be considered a new paradigm for understanding social cohesion, alongside established models such as multiculturalism and assimilationism, and their respective contributions to the educational field. The issue welcomes original research, systematic reviews, and theoretically grounded contributions that engage with multiculturalism, intercultural education, diversity management, social cohesion, and inclusive educational practice in formal and non-formal settings across all educational levels. Comparative, cross-national, and transdisciplinary perspectives are particularly encouraged, as are contributions documenting good practices and innovative approaches. By bringing these conversations into dialogue, this issue advances scholarly understanding and evidence-based policy reflection on one of the most pressing challenges facing European and global educational systems today. Instructions for authors: Authors interested in submitting a paper for this issue are asked to consult the journal's instructions for authors and submit their abstracts (maximum of 250 words, with a tentative title) through the abstracts system: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/app/socialinclusion/abstracts When submitting their abstracts, authors are also asked to confirm that they are aware that Social Inclusion is an open access journal with a publishing fee if the article is accepted for publication after peer-review (corresponding authors affiliated with our institutional members do not incur this fee). Open access: Readers across the globe will be able to access, share, and download this issue entirely for free. Corresponding authors affiliated with any of our institutional members (over 100 institutions worldwide) publish free of charge. Otherwise, an article processing fee will be charged to the authors to cover editorial costs. We defend that authors should not have to personally pay this fee and encourage them to check with their institutions if funds are available to cover open access publication costs. Further information about the journal's open access charges can be found here: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/socialinclusion/about/editorialPolicies#publicationFees Abstracts welcome until 15 December 2026.

items.title: Hydrotemporalities: Situating the spatial and temporal presence of water in historical, contemporary, and future perspectives
items.excerpt: Hydrotemporalities: Situating the spatial and temporal presence of water in historical, contemporary, and future perspectives: Student Conference, Early Career Researchers Opportunity The 'Hydro' in Hydrotemporalities draws from the Blue Humanities, a term coined by Steve Mentz in 2024, and more specifically from Astrida Neimanis' notion of Hydrofeminism...
items.fullDescription: Hydrotemporalities: Situating the spatial and temporal presence of water in historical, contemporary, and future perspectives: Student Conference, Early Career Researchers Opportunity The 'Hydro' in Hydrotemporalities draws from the Blue Humanities, a term coined by Steve Mentz in 2024, and more specifically from Astrida Neimanis' notion of Hydrofeminism and the collection Thinking with Water (eds. Astrida Neimanis, Cecilia Chen, and Janine MacLeod). As such, the 'Hydro' means to evoke and underline the ever growing importance of watery topics and posthumanism in the academic discourse, and is specifically indicative of the intersectional approach of the conference: As Mentz and Neimanis remind us, water is what connects all the world, water facilitates movement, growth, thinking, and loving, and water acts as a planetary archive. Further, we use 'Hydro' to mean water-based fluids of all kinds, in all its states, because we are interested in the different forms and meanings that it can take. It encompasses all bodies of water both artificial and natural, the polar caps, fog, rain, and even sewage. Temporalities refer to chronology; future, past, history, speculative time, and more. It can come to mean the temporal levels of a narrative, the way the past informs the present, the speculative presence of the future, scientific advancements and historical processes. Further, temporality necessitates a negotiation of place and space, seeing as the temporal must be situated within the spatial, in the tradition of Bakhtin's chronotopos. The spatial is not limited to physical places, but includes fictional/unreal and social/cultural spaces. In combining these two, we wish to uncover the role water and fluids play in the literary, historical, futuristic, scientific, and artistic chronologies and spaces of humanity, especially in regards to our current era of the Anthropocene and the changing climate. 'Hydro' situates itself in every aspect of the world. Our aim is to facilitate a productive exchange between different disciplines and give early career researchers the opportunity to build a supportive network. Disciplines and Topics can include but are not limited to: cultural and literary studies linguistics historical and archaeological perspectives art and art history natural sciences, such as biology, geology, ecology, and more philosophy, sociology, and political science geography narrative structures/cyclical narratives materiality and representation of water reconsidering the legacy of slavery/discussions of the middle passage water in all its states (steam/ice/fluid) ecocritical readings the polar caps/arctic imaginaries climate change/climate fiction the Anthropocene/posthumanism We welcome submissions from all kinds of early career researchers at BA, MA, and early PhD level. All disciplines are encouraged, as long as your idea fits the topic. The conference will be held in English. You may submit abstracts to present a paper you've already written or a paper in progress, but you can also send in concepts of a workshop, or any kind of creative presentation, such as fiction, art, movies, or music. items.title: [Edited book] Handbook of National Revolutions. National Revolutions in the World: Theories, Practices, International Relations
items.excerpt: Beginning in the nineteenth century, the world witnessed the emergence of national movements that advocated the construction of states founded upon the historical and cultural identity of peoples, as well as upon their independence and strategic autonomy. This wave, which manifested itself most prominently in the European revolutions of 1848, the so-calle...
items.fullDescription: Beginning in the nineteenth century, the world witnessed the emergence of national movements that advocated the construction of states founded upon the historical and cultural identity of peoples, as well as upon their independence and strategic autonomy. This wave, which manifested itself most prominently in the European revolutions of 1848, the so-called "Springtime of the Peoples," produced a long-term historical impact - according to the principle of the longue durée - that influenced world political history in the decades that followed. This phenomenon was of enormous importance in the Western political sphere, having its precursors in the American Revolution and in the political epic of South American Bolivarianism, and gaining momentum from 1848 onward with the emergence of a whole series of European national movements. With the First World War, and with the promotion by Woodrow Wilson and the United States of the principle of "self-determination of peoples," the same idea experienced a revival which, through Turkish Kemalism and the formation of the Chinese nationalist movement, extended into the non-Western world. Non-Western forms of this type of movement, in turn, had important precursors in anti-colonial movements, which, like European national movements, sought to secure independence and autonomy for broad sectors of the world subjected to foreign domination of an economic and extractive nature. During the twentieth century, the idea of national independence assumed various ideological and political forms, eventually giving rise to different theories of national autonomy and sovereignty, such as Mao Zedong's "Three Worlds Theory." At the same time, the rise of communist revolutions and of the world socialist camp revitalized this political idea, generating new formulations of theories of national revolution. With this call for papers, we intend to collect contributions on the theme of national revolutions in the West and the East, considered both from a theoretical perspective - by examining the political thought of the authors who promoted these movements, as well as the movements themselves - and from the perspective of the relations among these movements and the elaboration of a political theory of coexistence among these political projects. We also intend to focus on the theories and practices of these movements from the perspective of international relations, both by analyzing national revolutions within the international context, in diplomatic and strategic terms, and by addressing the theoretical elaboration of an international order founded upon national independence. A non-exhaustive list of topics that may be addressed includes: Jacobinism and the emergence of the idea of national revolution in Europe The American Revolution and the national-revolutionary paradigm Bolivarianism and national revolution in Spanish America 1848 and the transformation of the national idea in Europe Mazzini and the theory of nationalities The Italian Risorgimento and its relationship with the great powers Bonapartism and national revolutions Self-determination of peoples and the international order after the First World War Kemalism and the Turkish national revolutionù The Soviet Revolution and the issue of nationalities Chinese nationalism and national revolution in the thought of Sun Yat-sen Nationalism and anti-imperialism in anti-colonial liberation movements Mao Zedong and the theory of national revolution National revolution and internationalism in Marxist and communist thought National sovereignty, the balance of power, and the international order National identity and international relations theory National movements and the opposition to a bipolar and unipolar world National movements and anti-colonial struggles in Africa Arab nationalism and movements for emancipation in the Middle East Indian nationalism and the struggle for independence National and revolutionary movements in twentieth-century Latin America Nationalisms in Southeast Asia and the dissolution of the colonial empire Proposals should contain a title, a brief summary or abstract of between 300 and 400 words, the author's email address, and a brief five-line CV. Proposals must be sent to the email address nationalrevolutionsintheworld@gmail.com The deadline for submitting proposals is December 31, 2026. Accepted proposals will be announced starting January 31, 2027, and editorial instructions for preparing the book chapter will be provided. The deadline for submitting the final version of the chapters will be a date to be determined in the first quarter of 2027. The monograph containing the selected and submitted book chapters will subsequently be published, following corrections and comments by the coordinators. The monograph is expected to be published by an international academic publishing house. Coordinators: Orazio Maria Gnerre (Institute for the History of the Italian Risorgimento) Ruikai Xue (Beijing International Studies University)

items.fullDescription: How is everyone doing? At a routine meeting of the Editorial Board of this journal in March 2026, this innocuous question erupted into disquiet, tension, unease. Speaking from vastly different parts of the world, there was an unmistakable sense of a planet slipping beyond available comprehension and unplugging us from work and life routines. As wars in the Middle East expand and fires spread from apartment blocks reduced to rubble to bombed oil refineries and shipping corridors, profound geopolitical, personal, even psychic rifts leave us grasping for the language and feel of the moment, the falling apart of things, the zeitgeist of an endangered now.

items.title: Animal Studies Across Disciplines
items.location: Arizona State University · Arizona State University
items.excerpt: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pe...
items.fullDescription: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pervasive pollution. The effects of the Anthropocene have been caused by only a small percentage of the world's population, yet those living in the Global South disproportionately suffer the consequences. The Anthropocene, then, is just as much a social problem as it is an environmental issue. Despite the centrality of animals to planetary health, however, nonhuman life often remains peripheral to discussions of climate and environmental sustainability, even as industrial agriculture drives deforestation and carbon emissions, species extinction destabilizes ecosystems, and the increasing emergence of zoonotic diseases-Covid-19 and Hantavirus among them-reveals the profound interdependence of human, animal, and environmental health. At the same time, dominant responses to environmental crises, which made possible the conditions of crisis in the first place, tend to privilege scientific discovery and technological innovation while neglecting the cultural narratives, entrenched biases, and networks of power that shape human-animal relationships.. To that end, imagining more just and hospitable futures requires new interdisciplinary approaches that recognize animals and interspecies relations as critical to collective flourishing and environmental sustainability. The Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium will bring together scholars, artists, students, animal professionals, and community members across the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences to discuss animals and multispecies futures. The symposium is designed not only as a scholarly gathering, but as the start of a long-term collaborative network capable of shaping future research, public humanities work, community partnerships, and environmental dialogue. The inaugural Spring 2027 Symposium will center on the keyword "care," inviting participants to analyze how different disciplines, professions, and communities define and mobilize care in relation to animals, multispecies justice, and environmental stewardship. In doing so, the Symposium will evaluate practices of protection and responsibility alongside the violences and inequalities that shape life across species. For example, how might a humanities scholar, veterinarian, ecologist, or activist understand and practice care differently, and what might each learn from the knowledge, methods, and questions of the others? How might regional, place-based, and communal forms of knowledge offer different ways of understanding our relationships and responsibilities to animals? How is care negotiated when the welfare of an individual animal comes into conflict with the preservation of a population, species, or ecosystem? What might care mean for animals such as insects, whose small size, vast numbers, and frequent classification as pests or disease vectors complicate familiar practices of care? How do animals care for themselves, one another, and members of other species, and what might these practices teach us about caring for each other and the more-than-human world? The Symposium invites participants to consider what becomes possible when different ways of knowing and relating to animals are brought into conversation, and how such exchanges might expand our understanding and practice of care across species. Possible topics include: Regional approaches to Animal Studies and human-animal relations (e.g. desert ecologies, southern studies, the arctic, etc.) Global and transnational approaches to Animal items.title: Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy
items.excerpt: The Journal for the New Narratives in the History of Philosophy (JNNHP) invites submissions for its special on Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy, to be published in Fall 2027. Derrick Bell, the founder of Critical Race Theory, produced one of the most innovative, insightful, and transformative ideas in the 20th century. His philosophical...
items.fullDescription: The Journal for the New Narratives in the History of Philosophy (JNNHP) invites submissions for its special on Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy, to be published in Fall 2027. Derrick Bell, the founder of Critical Race Theory, produced one of the most innovative, insightful, and transformative ideas in the 20th century. His philosophical insights continue to challenge how western liberal nations contend with questions of civil rights, human rights, immigration, policing, and education. Recent conservative attacks focused on Critical Race Theory (CRT) in the U.S, Canada, and England assert, albeit erroneously, that CRT is a Marxist and communist ideology that seeks to supplant western values and the ethos of liberal democracy. Contrary to these fallacious attacks, Bell's textbook Race, Racism, and American Law is amongst the first law textbooks to give a comprehensive view of how racism shaped the development of American law and race relations. In this regard, CRT draws heavily on a tradition of Africana philosophy from slavery through the 20th century. It challenges, not only the supposed neutrality of U.S. law, but also the universality of western political ideals, and U.S. law as egalitarian. For example, Bell engaged Frederick Douglass's critiques of natural law theorists and abolitionists who read the American Constitution as a slave document. For Douglass, the Constitution is an economic contract that robs slaves of their labour and property rights. Drawing on Douglass' critique, Bell interrogated how economic interests have structured American law as an instrument for white class interests over Black claims for justice from slavery through the 20th century. Similarly, Bell engaged W.E.B DuBois's reading of American democracy that underscored how U.S. law in the 13 colonies suppressed African revolts while upholding slavery. Such legal resistance to African acts of liberation, Dubois argued, created paradoxes for American democracy and shaped how the legal system understood the Black freedom struggle. Following Dubois' analysis, Bell explored how the law is an ineffective tool for racial remediation when it comes to addressing social injustices that confront Black life. Bell also engaged Malcolm X's critiques of the Reconstruction era civil rights and 1960 civil rights amendments as pyrrhic victories. This inspired Bell to think about how civil rights function as symbolic victories while ensuring racism is a permanent fixture of American democracy. Given Bell's extensive engagement with 18th-20th century Africana philosophy, this special seeks to consider Bell's work within Africana philosophy. As such, the special welcomes essays that focus on Bell's work as philosophical historiography and inquiry into Black life and its relation to democracy as part of the long tradition of Africana philosophy. The special seeks contributions that address the following themes: Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black history. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black legal theory. Derrick Bell and the Black Nationalist and the Black Radical Tradition. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black Education. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of contemporary society and issue of civil rights. Essays must be submitted to https://journal.lib.uoguelph.ca/index.php/nnhp/about/submissions Deadline for Essay Submission: January 7th, 2027. Papers will be considered after January 7th, 2027. The Co-lead Guest Editors for this Special are Drs. Dalitso Ruwe (Queens University), Adebayo Oluwayomi (West Chester University), Andrew Soto (Hartnell College). For questions about the Special, please contact: derrickbellspecial@gmail.com JNNHP is an open-access online journal committed to publishing papers on underrepresented figures or themes in the history of philosophy, both Western and non-Western traditions, from the ancient period to the mid-20th century. JNNHP accepts papers in English and French. Papers should be no more than 10000 words. JNNHP also seeks to highlight relevant translations, archival work or new editions of primary texts in progress. We will publish selections from such works, with critical notes and contextual introductions.

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals The editorial and scientific board of the journal Co-herencia invites researchers, professors, and scholars affiliated with national or international institutions to submit proposals for thematic issues/dossiers, and to apply to serve as Guest Scientific Editors for Volume 25, Issue 48 (covering the period January-June 2028). Presentation and Scientific Scope of the Journal Co-herencia Co-herencia is an indexed scientific journal, published biannually, under Diamond Open Access with a CC BY 4.0 license, and edited by the School of Arts and Humanities at EAFIT University. Indexed in major international databases such as Scopus (Arts & Humanities, Q2 SJR), Co-herencia ensures methodological rigor, double-blind peer review, and high ethical publishing standards. The journal is published in Spanish, English, and Portuguese. Published without interruption since 2004, the journal aims to serve as a forum for interdisciplinary discussion on the contributions of the humanities and the arts to the shaping of a thoughtful, critical, and deliberative community. Its scope and thematic axes are concentrated mainly on: Literary Studies: Literary theory; Literary genres; Classical tradition; Hermeneutics; Canon, criticism, and history of literature in the Americas; Writing and orality; Translation; Reception; Literary creation; Semiotics; Editing studies; Journalism and literature; Applied literature. Philosophical Studies: Critical theory and social philosophy; Ethics; Political philosophy; Aesthetics; Epistemology; Philosophy of science and technology; Philosophy of mind; Cosmology; Philosophy of language; Argumentation theory; Rhetoric; Phenomenology; Philosophical hermeneutics; Ontology; Conceptual analysis; History of philosophy. Historical Studies: Historiography; Theory and philosophy of history; Methodology of history; Intellectual history; Conceptual history; Cultural history; Social and political history; History of knowledge; National and Latin American history; Global history; Colonial history; Memory and history; Historical geography and cartography; Imagination, speculation, and historical narratives. Arts: Mediality, transmediality, and intermediality; Creative industries; Musicology; History of music; Material and visual culture; Curatorship and museography; Sociology of the arts; Interartistic relations; Avant-gardes and artistic movements; Canon, criticism, and history of the arts in the Americas. Humanistic Studies in Dialogue with the Social Sciences: Critical discourse analysis; Plain language; Digital humanities; Cultural studies; Research-Creation; Philosophical and historical anthropology; Human geography; Environmental humanities; Medical humanities; Digital humanities; Public humanities; Qualitative analysis of quantitative methods; Clinical sociology; Studies on violence, peace, and reconciliation; Communication studies with a humanistic approach; Gender studies. Requirements for Submitting Proposals In keeping with international editorial best practices in the field of Arts and Humanities (diverse impact, editorial exogamy, international outreach, and analytical rigor), proposals submitted by candidates for guest editors must be presented in a single document (PDF or Word), written in Spanish, English, or Portuguese, and must include, in detail, the following five sections: Title of the thematic issue: it should be concise, clear, conceptually strong, and reflect the central problem to be addressed. Thematic presentation and theoretical grounding (500 to 1,000 words): propose a conceptual delimitation and a definition of the object of study, the core question, or the problematizing axis of the dossier. The proposal should also detail the disciplinary or interdisciplinary frameworks, indicating how the theme and approach engage with the journal's scientific scope. Justification and academic relevance (500 to 1,000 words): include a synthesis of the state of the art and a clear account of the novelty and relevance of the proposal within the contemporary debate in the arts and humanities. This section should ideally state the potential impact and interest the issue will generate within the international research community. Scientific biography of the prospective guest editors: a team of two to three guest editors with diverse institutional affiliations is recommended. For each team member, please indicate: full name, current institutional affiliation, highest academic degree, ORCID iD, and a summary (max. 300 words) of their research lines, ongoing projects, and recent publications in the thematic area of the proposal. List of prospective authors and articles: as evidence of the commitment to attracting original manuscripts, this section of the proposal must list between 3 and 6 potential or pre-invited authors of recognized standing or relevant emerging trajectory for the thematic issue. For each anticipated contribution, please provide: the author's full name, institutional affiliation, tentative article title, and a brief abstract (100-200 words). All manuscripts resulting from the call for the selected proposal must undergo double-blind peer review. Guest editors commit to actively participating in the preselection of manuscripts, suggesting qualified reviewers, and drafting a presentation/introduction for the dossier. Timeline for the Open Call and the Editorial Process Opening of the call for thematic issue proposals: September 1, 2026. Deadline for submission of thematic issue proposals: January 10, 2027. Evaluation of proposals by the scientific board and notification of results: January 25, 2027. Public launch of the call for the selected proposal: January 31, 2027. Deadline for submission of articles for the thematic dossier: May 31, 2027. Peer review and revision process: June-November 2027. Early publication of revised articles: October 2027-January 2028. Copyediting, XML-JATS markup, and digital layout: November 2027-February 2028. Official publication (Vol. 25, No. 48, January-June 2028): February-March 2028. How to Submit Proposals Complete proposals must be submitted electronically to the journal's official email (co-herencia@eafit.edu.co) or processed through the Co-herencia journal's OJS (Open Journal System) platform, attaching the document (PDF or Word) with the required information, using the subject line "Application for Thematic Dossier Vol. 25-48 - [Short title of the proposal]." Contacts for Further Information Editorial team of the journal Co-herencia: coherencia@eafit.edu.co Editorial assistant: Liam Agudelo Calle lagudeloc@eafit.edu.co Editor-in-chief: Andrés Vélez-Posada avelezp6@eafit.edu.co

items.fullDescription: Over recent decades, decadence studies has moved beyond earlier identifications of decadence with the Western European literary and artistic canon of the fin de siècle . Recent scholarship has, for example, developed new critical approaches to decadence, from translation studies to affect and sensory studies to postcolonial theory; illuminated the global dimensions of decadence; traced its afterlives and new literary histories; and examined its significance across diverse artistic and sociocultural practices, from food and fashion to performance and popular media. Taken together, these efforts underline the continued resonance of decadence as a capacious and multifaceted phenomenon for thinking about the many faces of modernity.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS First International Congress in Humanities - Texts, Images and Communities: "Body, Age and Gender" Org. HUM-TIC Research Group, University of Madeira, 17-18 June 2017 The way in which the body, age and gender shape human experiences is one of the most pressing challenges facing contemporary societies. Today, more than ever, there is a need to build fairer, more equitable and sustainable communities, which are in a state of continuous development and adaptation and which face limitations and obstacles. Some of these are long-standing and deeply rooted, whilst others are new and not very well known. A multidisciplinary approach to the cultural and social constructs of the body - and the multiple levels at which it functions as a generator of meaning - is therefore imperative. The proposed lines of research, both in their contemporary context and in terms of their cultural and historical foundations, fall within the core mission of the Humanities Research Group - Texts, Images and Communities (HUM-TIC). This event fosters free, informed discussion, driven by dialogue across the Humanities. This is the first International Congress organised by the HUM-TIC Research Group, Faculty of Arts and Humanities at the University of Madeira. It is an in-person event, which will take place at the Colégio dos Jesuítas, at the University of Madeira's Rectorate building in Funchal. The conference aims to explore one of HUM-TIC's main thematic areas - Body, Age and Gender - from a dialogical and transdisciplinary perspective. In this context, proposals of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, are welcome across the Humanities. These may include, among others, Art, Communication, Culture, Design, History, Linguistics, Literature, Psychology and Sociology. Discussion Topics (some suggestions): - Discourses, narratives and representations of the body, age and gender. - The body, space and territoriality: real, symbolic and imaginary places. - Rethinking the Human: AI and representations of the body, age and gender. - Aesthetics of the body, beauty and ugliness, the monstrous and the abject. - Building Self and the Other in different cultural contexts. - Stages of life: representations, experiences and intergenerational relationships. - Double standards of ageing in a consumer society. - Embodiment: inner and outer, personal and social, physical and idealised. - Body and gender: sexuality, emotions, ethics, violence. - Myths, stereotypes and imagined representations of the body, age and gender. - Ecologies of the body and environmental humanities. - Gender-based violence in the digital sphere. - The manosphere and social media impact. - Intersectionality and multiple forms of discrimination. - Gender, natural disasters and climate change. items.title: "Loving Roland Barthes: An Interdisciplinary Conference"
items.location: Mobile, Alabama · University of South Alabama
items.excerpt: Call for Papers: "Loving Roland Barthes" University of South Alabama (Mobile, AL) October 14-16, 2027 Loving [Barthes], doing so in a certain fashion against the age [. . .], can only be a responsible way of living: it inevitably leads the subject who does so and says so to posit himself in his time according to the injunctions of his desire and not accor...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: "Loving Roland Barthes" University of South Alabama (Mobile, AL) October 14-16, 2027 Loving [Barthes], doing so in a certain fashion against the age [. . .], can only be a responsible way of living: it inevitably leads the subject who does so and says so to posit himself in his time according to the injunctions of his desire and not according to those of his sociality. -Roland Barthes, "Loving Schumann" Proposals for panels and papers are invited for a conference entitled "Loving Roland Barthes: Celebrating the Fiftieth Anniversary of the Publication of A Lover's Discourse: Fragments ," to be hosted by the University of South Alabama's Department of English and held at the historic Malaga Inn in downtown Mobile, city of the oldest Mardi Gras in the U.S. As conference organizers, we envision a relatively concentrated event in which scholars working in various disciplines and artists working in various genres will present new ideas about Roland Barthes, A Lover's Discourse , and his adjacent texts. This conference celebrates a peculiar form of love: an amorousness that compels the one faithful to "the specialty of [one's] desire" ( Lover's Discourse 20) to return again and again to Fragments d'un discours amoureux . Published in 1977 and translated a year later by Richard Howard as A Lover's Discourse: Fragments , Roland Barthes's tortured love song retains a strong attachment for scholars and artists alike. We might be tempted to call those strange lovers "amateurs." For, as Barthes reminded us, the word derives from "amator: one who loves and loves again" (Roland Barthes 52). Across the last five decades, the book has inspired not only articles and artwork but also autotheory, "an emergent discourse with historical precedents" (McLaughlin et al., Autotheory and Its Others 15). Often recognizable by its copious citations, autotheoretical practice pays homage to A Lover's Discourse: Fragments as one way of loving Barthes. Yet there is no limit to the modes of loving Barthes. For some, it might be collage, an assemblage of the very fragments that Barthes favored. For others, it might be singing a song (such as Annie Lennox's "No More 'I Love You's'") or writing notations (one of Barthes's preferred activities). For still others, it might be searching for "a little corner of sloth," "twiddl[ing one's] wound," or accepting "[t]he lover's fatal identity [. . .]: I am the one who waits" (Lover's Discourse 64, 161, 40). Whatever one's manner of loving Barthes, this conference invites scholars and artists to a celebration of A Lover's Discourse: Fragments . Contributions can take the form of traditional papers as well as of visual art, short film, skits, songs, and other Barthesian types of work or play. Possible topics include but are not limited to the following: · Figures and images in A Lover's Discourse: Fragments ; · Fragments and citations; · "[C]ontrolled accident" ("An Almost Obsessive Relation to Writing Instruments" 182) and the text's other structural and organizational features; · Barthes's use of Goethe's Werther; · "[T]he history of tears," "a scenography of waiting," and other extrapolations from the text (180, 37); · Relationships between this text and other works by Barthes, especially from the 1970s; · Barthes's (post)structuralist discussions of substitution, replication, and supplement; · Translation and differences between the French and English versions of the text; · Autotheory and other experimental, creative-critical practices inspired by Barthes; · (Loving) parodies of A Lover's Discourse ; · Anachronism in A Lover's Discourse both at the point of publication and now. As much as we trust that this conference will generate exciting new art and scholarship, we also hope to foster a substantial exchange of ideas and perspectives among all participants as well as personal interaction among scheduled presentations. Therefore, conference panels will be scheduled sequentially rather than concurrently so that all participants will be able to attend all panels, and we strongly encourage participants to stay for the duration of the conference. We believe that much good work will come from the conference, and we hope to assemble a collection of that work in the months following the conference in order to share it with the widest possible audience. Kicking off the conference will be a keynote address by Tufts professor John Lurz, author of The Barthes Fantastic: Literature, Criticism, and the Practice of Language . Please submit proposals of 350-500 words by email to Becky McLaughlin (email address: bmclaugh@southalabama.edu) and Eric Daffron (email address: edaffron@ramapo.edu) or by snail mail to Becky McLaughlin, Department of English, HUMB 240, University of South Alabama, Mobile, AL 36688. Due date: January 15, 2027.

items.title: Black Is...Black Is: Story as Construction and Celebration of Identity
items.location: Howard University · The Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association at Howard University
items.excerpt: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities an...
items.fullDescription: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities and identifications, and it cuts against the second half of his title, which suggests Blackness in terms of negation, evasion, and minimization. His articulation becomes not just an evocation of Black identifications but a creation of what a Black identity can be. Riggs continues a conversation with Ralph Ellison, Ama Ata Aidoo, Toni Morrison, Stuart Hall, and centuries of international Black thought. By doubling down on the "is" and considering contradictory, harmonious, and contrapuntal accounts of the many ways Blackness is and can be, the Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association hopes to join this dialogue with its March 25-26, 2027 conference. We invite papers that contemplate how storytelling produces and shapes Black identities as much as it narrates them, forming, revising, and improvising senses of self and community. This conference also does commemorative work. We are honoring the career of Dr. Jimisha Relerford, a graduate of our program and member of the Howard community who passed recently. Her dissertation broke critical ground in its study of Black women's satire. We thus encourage the submission of papers about Black satire, especially Black women's work in the genre. Writers such as Leone Ross, Danzy Senna, Fran Ross, and Zadie Smith, all of whom were discussed in Dr. Relerford's dissertation, use satire to comment on and transform notions of Blackness. We hope to continue Dr. Relerford's project by reflecting on how storytellers work within this genre to talk about identity. We additionally encourage studies of Afrofuturist and speculative Black texts in reference to our organization's namesake, a pillar in Afrofuturist study. In addition to recognizing the intellectual impacts of Drs. Relerford and Hampton, this conference serves as a milestone, marking the tenth conference our organization has hosted in honor of Black literary study. Given Black academia and HBCUs's influence on identity and storytelling around it, we also welcome papers pondering scholarly impacts on identity as seen in criticism, productions, and protest. items.fullDescription: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, frames are negotiated, shifted, and sometimes shattered in the movement between languages and cultures. They are the selective filters that highlight certain elements while relegating others to the background, the conceptual structures that allow us to categorize, interpret, and communicate complex realities.

items.fullDescription: (Re)Generation of the Nonhuman: Nature and Text in Dialogue The last decade has seen a surge in interdisciplinary scholarship, exploring the nonhuman in a broad range of critical perspectives. Whether through Glenworth et al (2024)'s conservationist prism which contextualizes 'Rewilding' as a way of restoring 'non-human autonomy'; or perhaps, through Bram Büscher (2021)'s capitalist reflections on nature's alienation and entanglement, both of which are recent approaches that seek to champion the cause of 'decentering the human in favor of a concern for the nonhuman' (Grusin, 2015: 1), we see a growing pace of intersectionality within which nature and literature are brazenly intertwined. Often suggested as a repressed generation of ecological beings, either of subaltern considerations or anthropomorphic (de)constructions, the nonhuman, whether plants, animals, or ecosystems, has continued to fit the bill for a contemporary kind of critical and textual narrative that urgently needs to undergo transformation through a process of generation, regeneration or auto-generation, after decades of being consistently synonymous with the image of depletive degeneration. David Abram (1996:22-23) describes the geographical space of this non-human depletion of nature as a biosphere of 'nonregenerative' decline, which in his views, has resulted in a variation of problems for humans: epidemics (including immune diseases and cancers) or perhaps, pandemics like the 2019 COVID which postdates Abram's study; or mental disorders. In the face of today's climate change and biodiversity loss, this collection proposes a constructive way of exploring literature's capacity to both reflect (on) the devastation of the natural world and, more importantly, provide imaginative models for its regeneration. Drawing on ecocritical theory, environmental humanities, animal studies, posthumanism, and new materialism, this collection invites papers that trace how literary texts can challenge anthropocentric templates, (re)imagining a textual world in which the nonhuman is seen as an active element with agency, living autonomously or forging a reciprocal connection with the human world. Scholars in French and Francophone Studies are invited to submit abstracts for a Bloomsbury critical collection exploring the relationship between literature and the nonhuman through interdisciplinary perspectives. Early and mid-career scholars are especially encouraged to submit. Authors must have a PhD. Papers can engage with, but are not limited to, the following themes: Ecocriticism (this includes, but are not limited to, a combination of ecocritical theories with other theories with the use of the prefix 'eco', e.g., ecofeminism, ecophenomenology, ecopoetics, ecocultural identities, ecoqueer, etc) Environmental Humanities Geocriticism Green Negritude Studies Green Cultural Studies Deep Ecology Dark Ecology Collapsology Spiralism Speciesism Blue Humanities Landscape Ecology Material ecocriticism Soundscape studies Animal Studies Race and Species Critical Plant Studies Multispecies Studies Indigenous Ecologies Black Ecologies Anthropocene Plantationocene Nonhuman Metamorphosis Afro-Caribbean Cosmologies Archipelagic Studies Environmental Aesthetics Ecological Kinship Créolisation and Ecological Relations Nonhuman Temporalities Decolonial Ecologies Environmental Justice Ecological Memory Please send proposals of 250-300 words and a 150 word biography to Israel Eweka at isreweka2019@outlook.com and Savannah DiGregorio at savannah.digregorio@asu.edu by January 25th, 2027. Notifications of acceptance will be sent by the end of February 2027. If accepted, full chapter drafts of approximately 6,000-8,000 words, including notes, will be due by July 5th, 2027.

items.fullDescription: Dear Colleagues, We are pleased to invite you to contribute a chapter to our upcoming edited volume, Objective Function-Based Clustering: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications, to be published by Springer Nature, the largest global scientific, technical, and medical ebook publisher. The volume will be published under the Unsupervised and Semi-Supervised Learning series (https://tinyurl.com/4mfur7zr) . It will be available in both print and ebook format by late 2027 on SpringerLink, a leading science portal that includes more than 8.4 million documents, an ebook collection with more than 275,000 titles, journal archives digitized back to the first issues in the 1840s, and over 30,000 conference proceedings. Synopsis of the Volume =================== Clustering, the unsupervised classification of patterns into groups, is one of the most critical tasks in exploratory data analysis. The primary goals of clustering include gaining insight into, classifying, and compressing data. Clustering has a long and rich history across scientific disciplines, including anthropology, biology, medicine, psychology, statistics, mathematics, engineering, and computer science. As a result, numerous clustering algorithms have been proposed since the early 1950s. Among these, objective function-based algorithms (e.g., batch k-means, online k-means, k-harmonic means, spherical k-means, and fuzzy c-means) are especially popular in modern scientific and engineering applications due to their optimization-based formulation and computational efficiency. This volume aims to summarize the state of the art in objective function-based clustering. Topics of Interest ============== Topics of interest include: Hard clustering algorithms Fuzzy, probabilistic, and possibilistic clustering algorithms Information-theoretic clustering algorithms Neural clustering algorithms Metaheuristic clustering algorithms Constrained clustering algorithms Approximate clustering algorithms Parallel and distributed clustering algorithms Dissimilarity and similarity functions for clustering Objective functions for clustering Initialization of clustering algorithms Convergence properties of clustering algorithms Robustness of clustering algorithms Algorithms for clustering high-dimensional data Evaluation of clustering algorithms Visualization of clustering algorithms Software and hardware implementations of clustering algorithms Applications of clustering algorithms Important dates ---------------------- Submission of abstracts: February 1, 2027 Notification of initial editorial decisions: February 15, 2027 Submission of full-length chapters: May 15, 2027 Notification of final editorial decisions: July 1, 2027 Submission of revised chapters: October 1, 2027 Publication of the volume: Late 2027 Submission Instructions ==================== Each contributed chapter is expected to present a novel research study, a comparative study, or a survey of the literature. All submissions, including abstracts and full-length chapters, must be done via EasyChair: https://easychair.org/ conferences/?conf=ofbc2027 There will be no publication fees for the accepted chapters. Resources for chapter authors ------------------------------ -------------- Book publishing policies: https://tinyurl.com/2r66erx9 Manuscript guidelines: https://tinyurl.com/mpcd9ype Book chapter templates: Microsoft Word: https://tinyurl.com/4swdmd3x LaTeX: https://tinyurl.com/jbyz5nx2 LaTeX (Overleaf): https://tinyurl.com/22sk4aec LaTeX best practice guidelines: https://tinyurl.com/2zvaje5f About the Editor ============== M. Emre Celebi (https://tinyurl.com/mtw6dx39) received his B.S. degree in Computer Engineering from the Middle East Technical University (Ankara, Turkey) in 2002. He received his M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in Computer Science and Engineering from the University of Texas at Arlington (Arlington, TX, USA) in 2003 and 2006, respectively. He is currently a Professor and the Chair of the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Central Arkansas. Celebi has pursued research in artificial intelligence and image processing, focusing on medical image analysis, color image processing, and partitional clustering. He has worked on several projects funded by the US National Science Foundation and the US National Institutes of Health, publishing over 180 articles in reputable journals and conference proceedings. As of October 2026, his work has received nearly 25,000 citations with an h-index of 65 (GS: https://tinyurl.com/3snjm8at). According to a 2026 Stanford University study (https://tinyurl.com/236hx3m2) , based on the composite citation index (an indicator of citation impact), in the single-year (2025) and career-long impact categories, Celebi ranked 1277th and 942nd, respectively, out of 517,648 artificial intelligence and image processing researchers worldwide. Celebi has published 12 edited volumes since 2012, all but one with Springer Nature. The artificial intelligence/machine learning volumes he edited to date include Partitional Clustering Algorithms (Springer Nature, 2015, https://tinyurl.com/3yezehcw) and Unsupervised Learning Algorithms (Springer Nature, 2016, https://tinyurl.com/4z8hdevh). He is also a series editor of two Springer Nature book series: Unsupervised and Semi-Supervised Learning (since 2017) and Signals and Communication Technology (since 2019). items.fullDescription: Aviation has long captured the cultural imagination as a symbol of freedom, technological progress, and global connectivity. Yet it has also provided the backdrop for stories of crime, transgression, mystery, and fear. From hijackings and sabotage to smuggling, cybercrime, and high-profile investigations, aviation crime has inspired enduring narratives across popular culture, shaping public perceptions of safety, risk, and justice. This symposium invites scholars, practitioners, researchers, writers, and creators to explore aviation crime as both a lived reality and a cultural phenomenon. We welcome contributions examining the representation and interpretation of aviation crime in popular culture, including film, television, literature, digital media, journalism, true crime, gaming, and public memory. Bringing together diverse perspectives, the symposium seeks to examine how aviation crime is represented, experienced, remembered, and imagined. We welcome papers from researchers across the academic spectrum and encourage papers from postgraduate researchers and early career researchers. Topics can include, but are not limited to: • From headlines to Hollywood-Aviation Crime in Film, Television and Popular Media • Who is DB Cooper?-Folklore, Myth and Unsolved Mysteries • The Investigation continues-Journalism, True Crime and Public Memory • Picture Perfect Crime-Art, Illustration and Visual Culture • Paperbacks in the Seat Pocket-Fiction, Crime Writing and Literary Culture • To be continued…-Comics, Graphic Novels and Popular Print • If You See Something, Say Something-Security, Surveillance and Risk • Going Viral-Digital Media, Social Networks and Online Communities • Surely, you can't be serious?-Humour, Parody and Camp • Crime at 30,000ft-New Directions in Aviation Crime Studies • Flygirl, Femme Fatale, Fugitive-Women in aviation crime fiction and film To submit - please visit our portal to submit your 200-word abstract by 28 February 2027: Submission portal : https://unesurveys.au1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_8jjzaWnS732QsFE To register (free) : https://unesurveys.au1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_7TGWUYZidtlxVLU Please email queries to: info@aviationcultures.org

items.fullDescription: Introduction: I teach composition to both undergraduate upperclassmen and first-year graduate students at my university. In both these classes, I have found the curricular material available to me lacking in a couple of ways: either it's outdated or it's intended for doctoral-level readers who already have prior knowledge and a shared vocabulary. That makes reading for these classes in any meaningful way prohibitively difficult for many students. The threshold concepts that many of us who have taught writing for awhile share remain barriers for less experienced students or entry-level teachers. This collection will help those teachers who don't yet have tons of experience in the classroom or with doctoral-level research in the field. It bridges that gap. As editor, I want students or early-career teachers who access this collection to feel more confident in being well-informed about disciplinary conversations and better prepared to apply the real-world knowledge of more experienced teachers in their own classrooms. They should have a resource that doesn't require hours of wading through eye-crossing disciplinary jargon. This collection will use plain, easy-to-understand language. Objective: In short, purposeful chapters, this collection will help new and future teachers of writing better understand terminology or concepts in a way that fosters deep learning for themselves and application in their future classrooms. This book is, primarily, borne out of a need for a more context-appropriate textbook in an undergraduate and a master's-level introduction to composition studies course. Audience: The audience for this collection is upper-level undergraduate students and first-year graduate students just beginning to conceptualize what it means to teach writing at the high school or college level. In addition, this collection could be useful for teachers in other disciplines looking for clarification in writing pedagogy approaches outside their experience or instructional librarians tasked with supporting writing curriculum. Proposal submission procedure: Please complete and submit this form. Important Dates: Priority proposal submission deadline: December 1, 2026 Final proposal submission deadline: March 1, 2027 Submissions due end of 2027 Revisions due summer 2028 Early 2029 publication goal Send questions to: Dr. Jill Parrott, Professor of English Eastern Kentucky University jill.parrott@eku.edu Publishing info: Telling Teaching Writing is an open educational resource (OER) published by EKU Libraries housed in Manifold, a resource for open publishing supported by The Open Education Network (OEN). For more information about the requirements, benefits, and drawbacks for OERs, please read the Unesco statement on Open Educational Resources. This collection will exhibit the values of accessibility, equity, and inclusivity that open resources allow. Generative AI Policy for Contributors: Contributors to this edited volume are expected to submit original work that reflects their own scholarship, interpretation, and writing. The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools (e.g., systems that produce text, images, or substantive content) to create, draft, or significantly revise any portion of a chapter is not permitted. Limited use of AI tools is acceptable for non-substantive purposes, such as proofreading, grammar correction, or general clarity improvements, provided that these tools do not generate new ideas, arguments, or original phrasing. Authors remain fully responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and originality of their submissions. By submitting a proposal, contributors affirm that their work will comply with this policy.

In-person presentations only. Featuring Orson Scott Card, award-winning author of Ender's Game and Speaker for the Dead, with keynote speakers Pat Gelsinger, Joan Slonczewski, and Ben John. ABOUT THE CONFERENCE Oral Roberts University invites proposals for AI and the Imagination from participants across disciplines and professions. We welcome research, critical reflection, creative work, and practical applications. Students, faculty, researchers, educators, industry professionals, practitioners, faith leaders, writers, and artists are encouraged to contribute. Artificial intelligence is reshaping how we learn, work, create, and understand ourselves. The conference brings together conversations that too often occur separately, offering an opportunity to share ideas and experiences, question assumptions, and consider how our choices today will shape the years ahead. Interdisciplinary contributions are particularly encouraged. CONFERENCE TRACKS AI and the Imagination How have we imagined artificial intelligence, and how is artificial intelligence changing imagination itself? This signature track welcomes work involving science fiction, fantasy, film, literature, art, storytelling, speculative futures, AI-assisted creativity, and the ways imaginative works can help us understand possible technological futures. AI, Theology, and Ethics What theological, philosophical, and ethical questions arise from increasingly capable artificial intelligence? This track welcomes work on Christian theology and AI, ethics, human dignity, personhood, moral agency, wisdom, responsibility, vocation, technology and faith, and related philosophical or religious questions. AI, Human Agency, and Formation How does AI change what it means to think, choose, act, develop, and become? This track explores human agency in an age of increasingly capable AI, including cognitive and agency offloading, judgment and decision-making, autonomy, dependence, human-AI relationships, meaning, purpose, identity, formation, and human flourishing. AI and Teaching and Learning How is AI changing education and the work of teaching and learning? Topics may include pedagogy, assessment, academic integrity, AI literacy and fluency, faculty development, student learning, educational technology, curriculum design, personalized learning, and emerging models of education. AI, Society, and the Human Future What does widespread AI mean for individuals, communities, institutions, and society? Topics may include work, economics, culture, politics, law, relationships, inequality, democracy, social institutions, public policy, and the broader consequences of AI for the human future. AI, Leadership, Strategy, and Governance How should leaders make decisions in an AI-rich environment? This track welcomes work addressing leadership, organizational strategy, institutional transformation, governance, policy, risk, workforce development, and responsible AI adoption. AI, Research, Discovery, and Innovation How is AI transforming the process of discovery and the creation of new knowledge? This track includes AI-enabled research, interdisciplinary research methods, scientific discovery, innovation, entrepreneurship, and emerging approaches to scholarship and creative inquiry. SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Please include: • Presentation title • A 250-500-word abstract outlining the topic, approach, and main contribution of the proposed presentation • Preferred conference track • Presenter name(s) and institutional or professional affiliation, if applicable • Contact email(s) • Whether you plan to read a paper or give a presentation using slides A full paper or slide deck is not required at the proposal stage. Email proposals by March 5, 2027, to either conference co-organizer: Dr. Andrew Lang Dean, College of Science and Engineering Senior Professor of Mathematics Oral Roberts University alang@oru.edu Dr. Mark Hall Dean, J.D. McKean Library Senior Professor of English Oral Roberts University mhall@oru.edu Proposals will be reviewed as they are received. Early submissions are encouraged. PRESENTATION FORMAT All presentations will be delivered in person. Standard sessions allow 15 minutes for presentation followed by 5 minutes for questions and discussion. Accepted abstracts will be included in the online conference program. The conference will not publish formal proceedings or full papers. REGISTRATION Registration is required for all attendees, including accepted presenters. Please consult the conference website for registration information, hotel recommendations, schedule updates, and additional details. FEATURED SPEAKERS Orson Scott Card Award-winning author of Ender's Game and Speaker for the Dead. Pat Gelsinger Executive chair and head of technology at Gloo, general partner at Playground Global, and former CEO of Intel and VMware. His career spans more than 45 years in engineering and technology leadership. Joan Slonczewski, PhD Award-winning science fiction author and Professor of Biology at Kenyon College. Their novels include A Door into Ocean, Brain Plague, The Highest Frontier, and Minds in Transit. Their work explores evolution, biotechnology, artificial intelligence, and the future of intelligent life. Ben John, PhD Chief Technology Officer of Digital Turbine and former Vice President of Engineering at Microsoft AI, where he led the Copilot data platform. He previously served as CTO of AppNexus and Xandr. We are imagining more than the future of AI. We are imagining who we will become. Come imagine it with us in Tulsa. Conference website: https://oru.edu/academics/cose/ai-and-the-imagination/

items.fullDescription: "Creators of Gothic fiction have always been swift to take advantage of new media technologies", writes Joseph Campbell in Twenty-First Century Gothic, adding that "[t]he internet has proven to be no exception" (72). This special issue argues that horror storytelling on the internet - whether in the form of creepypasta (user-generated horror narratives that circulate online), collaborative digital storytelling universes, or multimodal digital narratives like podcasts, analog horror, and webseries - represents a vibrant contemporary evolution of the Gothic mode. Digital horror scholarship is a rich and rapidly expanding field, reflecting the increasing, and increasingly unsettling, centrality of the digital in our lives. Digital horror has been fruitfully interpreted through the lenses of digital culture and fan studies, as well as, recently, folklore and contemporary legend studies: Trevor Blank and Lynne McNeill's Slender Man Is Coming: Creepypasta and Contemporary Legends on the Internet (2018) positions Slender Man and other internet horror narratives as contemporary folklore, reading them in terms of community creation and ostensive practices, and Creepypasta, Digital Horror, and Legend Formation Across Interactive Media, a 2025 special issue of Contemporary Legend edited by Natalie Underberg Goode, picks up on the folkloric aspect of "'crowd-sourced' horror storytelling" and applies it to more recent digital horror phenomena (1). However, there is also a continuing critical tradition of reading digital horror as Gothic, from Isabella van Elferen's concept of the Cybergothic, which argues that "cyberspace is a spectral place haunted by the dualism of information and materiality" (2009, 99), to Jessica Balanzategui's delineation of the "digital Gothic" (2019) in the context of creepypasta narratives and Marc Olivier's concept of the "postdigital Gothic" (2021), which "calls attention to hidden architecture undergirding the virtual […] a vault of manuscripts buried beneath familiar interfaces" (323). Most recently, the 2026 International Gothic Association conference, Gothic Selves/Artificial Others, turned its attention to the Gothic aspects of AI technology, exploring "the intersections of Gothic literature, culture, and theory with artificial intelligence, automated creativity, and posthuman forms of subjectivity". Taken together, these approaches suggest the need to ask not simply how horror operates in digital media, but what happens when the distinctive structures, anxieties, and modes of participation of digital culture are understood through the Gothic. This special issue, then, foregrounds the specifically Gothic dimensions of digital horror, positioning this form of participatory, networked storytelling within a long Gothic tradition that extends from the 18th century to the present day. The volume explores how digital folklore reworks longstanding Gothic anxieties in contemporary modes, translating familiar structures of Gothic space, monstrosity, and uncertainty into the networked environment: the Backrooms, for instance, transpose the labyrinthine entrapment of the Gothic castle into vast, uncanny digital spaces, while internet-born monsters such as those catalogued by Line Henriksen in "A Short Bestiary of Creatures from the Web" (2013) emerge through processes of circulation, accumulation, and collective invention. The classic Gothic epistolary format is reimagined in forums like r/Nosleep (a subreddit for telling scary stories that purport to be true), wiki-style collaborative databases like the SCP Foundation, and found-footage web series, forms that invite audiences to participate in the reconstruction of events whose status as fictional or factual remains uncertain. This special issue asks how these narratives articulate contemporary anxieties around technological alienation, surveillance, epistemic uncertainty, unstable authorship, and the increasingly porous boundaries between reality and fiction. We welcome interdisciplinary contributions that explore digital horror through Gothic perspectives. Possible themes might include: - Digital horror folklore as Gothic storytelling - Nostalgia, remediation, materiality, lost media - Analog horror - Digital horror as epistolary Gothic - Alternate Reality Games and the boundaries between the screen and the world - AI horror, deepfakes, and algorithmic horror - Surveillance horror - Horror podcasts as Gothic storytelling - Digital hoaxes and curses - Dead media and the dead internet - Collaborative and crowdsourced storytelling - The postdigital Gothic and the digital as Gothic infrastructure Please submit proposals of ca. 500 words and brief biographies for consideration to both Elena Romea (University Carlos III of Madrid)) eromea@hum.uc3m.es and Erika Kvistad (University of South-Eastern Norway) erika.kvistad@usn.no by 1 March 2027 (include 'Gothic Studies' in the header). Completed articles are expected to be between 5,000-7,000 words. References Balanzategui, Jessica. "Creepypasta, 'Candle Cove', and the digital gothic". Visual Culture, 18.2 (2019), 187-208. Blank, Trevor and Lynne McNeill (eds). Slender Man Is Coming: Creepypasta and Contemporary Legends on the Internet. Utah State University Press, 2018. Campbell, Joseph. "Gothic Digital Technologies". In Twenty-First Century Gothic: An Edinburgh Companion, eds. Xavier Aldana Reyes and Maisha Wester. Edinburgh University Press, 2019. Henriksen, Line. "A Short Bestiary of Creatures from the Web". The Ashgate Research Companion to Paranormal Cultures, eds. Olu Jenzen and Sally R. Munt. Ashgate, 2013. The International Gothic Association. Gothic Selves/Artificial Others. [Call for papers] Hull Gothic, 2025. https://hullgothic.wordpress.com/cfp/ Olivier, Marc. "Postdigital Gothic". The Cambridge History of the Gothic, Volume 3: Gothic in the Twentieth and Twenty-First Centuries, eds. Catherine Spooner and Dale Townshend, Cambridge University Press, 2021. Underberg-Goode, Natalie. "Introduction to Creepypasta, Digital Horror, and Legend Formation Across Interactive Media". Creepypasta, Digital Horror, and Legend Formation Across Interactive Media, special issue of Contemporary Legend. 4.3 (2025), 1-15. van Elferen, Isabella. "Dances with Spectres: Theorising the Cybergothic". Gothic Studies, 11.1 (2009), 99-112.
