items.fullDescription: Third Culture: Studies in Global Childhoods and Cosmopolitan Identities is a new peer-reviewed journal dedicated to the study of cultural and social issues related to complex cosmopolitan identities arising from mobile global childhoods which transcend conventional categories of migrancy and diaspora. Acknowledging Benedict Anderson's well-established idea that the nation is an imagined community, the specific focus of this journal is on the large and growing number of people whose identities are formed by the experience of having lived in three or more different nations during their childhoods. This is because there is already a substantial body of scholarly work on issues of migrancy, diaspora, and bicultural identities, so this journal was established to explore the experiences, perspectives, representations, and cultural productions of people whose mobile global childhoods have produced more complex cosmopolitan identities. Our first issue was published in May 2026, and for our second issue we are now inviting submissions which include: Scholarly articles based on original research in the arts (particularly literature) and/or the social sciences Book reviews Autobiographical narratives Original pieces of creative writing Please see the submission guidelines on the journal website: https://journals.sta.uwi.edu/ojs/index.php/tc/about/submissions Deadline: March 31, 2027 Editorial contact: thirdculturejournal@gmail.com

The region's normative frameworks and public policies have incorporated the principles of inclusive e...
items.fullDescription: Introduction Thirty years on from the Salamanca Statement and Framework for Action on Special Needs Education (UNESCO, 1994), Latin America and the Caribbean have gone through a complex and challenging process towards building inclusive education systems. The region's normative frameworks and public policies have incorporated the principles of inclusive education to varying degrees, while curricular and pedagogical practices in classrooms continue to face tensions between the normative mandate and the actual conditions of implementation. This special issue of RECAP: Research in Education Curriculum and Pedagogy invites academics, researchers and teams to submit papers that critically examine the progress made, the challenges that persist and, in particular, what works in relation to inclusive education, special education and public policy in Latin American and Caribbean. Aim of the special issue To bring together original and rigorous research that provides evidence on the curricular and pedagogical transformations driven by inclusive education policy frameworks in Latin America and the Caribbean since 1994, with particular attention to practices, strategies and interventions that have demonstrated positive and sustainable outcomes. RECAP is part of AT-Journals (https://at-journals.com/). The guidelines for authors are available here (https://recap.at-journals.com/recap/index.php/description/about/submissions). Thematic areas Contributions are invited on, among others, the following themes: Normative frameworks and public policy on inclusive education and special education in the region. Policy implementation processes: gaps between normative design and classroom practice. Curricular transformations aimed at inclusion: universal design for learning, curricular adaptations and pedagogical flexibilisation. Initial and continuing teacher education for attending to diversity. Experiences and evidence on effective pedagogical practices (what works) in inclusive contexts. Inclusive education in rural contexts, indigenous peoples, Afro-descendant communities and migration. Family and community participation in inclusive education processes. Evaluation and monitoring of inclusion policies: indicators, information systems and accountability. Comparative studies across countries in the region. Perspectives of students with special educational needs, disabilities and intersecting identities on their own educational trajectories. Types of contributions Empirical research articles, systematic literature reviews, case studies and public policy analyses will be accepted. Manuscripts must comply with RECAP's editorial guidelines. Languages Manuscripts are accepted in Spanish* and English. *Spanish manuscripts will require - in an addition - an English abstract of 300-500 words. Additional support for first-time authors RECAP aims to encourage new researchers by providing additional support to those who are submitting for the first time to an international peer-reviewed academic journal. We offer by request up to two formative feedback reviews (including 1-to-1 tutorials) before the manuscript is sent for the peer-review process. Please see the key dates below: Key dates First time author/s additional support: November 2026 to January 2027 Please submit abstract and/or first draft for formative feedback adding in the subject - SEN (Special Educational Needs) special issue requesting formative feedback . Full manuscript submission deadline: 31st March 2027 Notification of first review outcomes: 30th June 2027 Estimated publication date: November 2027 Manuscript submission Manuscripts should be submitted through the RECAP platform (https://recap.at-journals.com/recap/index.php/description/index), indicating in the system that the contribution is for this special issue.

items.fullDescription: The third International Conference on Globalisation/Deglobalisation in Languages, Education, Culture and Communication (GLECC2027) is going to be held 27-29 July, 2027, Manchester, UK. The past two decades have witnessed remarkable advancements in the studies into Education, Second and Foreign Languages, Translation and Interpreting, Cultural Studies, and Communication. This growth, evident in both the number of active researchers and the volume of scholarly throughput and outcomes, can be largely attributed to the forces of globalisation. Consequently, adopting the globalisation perspective is timely and provides a natural framework for connecting these diverse yet interlinked disciplines. GLECC2027 aims to bring together researchers, educators, practitioners, and policymakers from the realms of education, foreign and second languages, cultural studies, translation, interpreting, and communication to disseminate research outcomes, share insights, discuss findings, exchange visions, and identify challenges and trends in an interactive and immersive multidisciplinary environment. This conference, notwithstanding the dissemination of works within individual and traditional discipline specified scopes, endeavours to break the subject silos. Papers and other contributions in Education, Second and Foreign Languages, Translation and Interpreting, Cultural Studies, or Communication, as well as contributions crossing the borders of traditional disciplines or emerged from frontier research, are welcome. The conference is organised by AT Publishing in association with its four journals namely, Research in Education Curriculum and Pedagogy: Global Perspectives (RECAP) [ISSN: 2977-1633]; New Perspectives on Languages (NPL) [ISSN: 3033-490X]; The International Journal of Chinese and English Translation & Interpreting (IJCETI) [ISSN: 2753-6149] and Recent Advances in Humanities Arts and Social Sciences (HASS) [ISSN: 2978-1345]. There is a "conference first" policy in place. Selected papers will be invited to further develop into full journal articles free of APCs. Conference proceedings will be published open access with an ISBN.

items.title: Resonances and Polysemy: Musical Forms and Meanings in the Literary Text.
items.excerpt: Between XVII.34 (2027): Resonances and Polysemy: Musical Forms and Meanings in the Literary Text. Editors : Stefano Franceschini (Roma Tre University), Fiorenzo Iuliano (University of Cagliari) Submission Deadline: 27 May 2027 Publication Date: 15 December 2027 In Chapter 25 of Thomas Mann's Doctor Faustus (1947), Mephistopheles promises the protagonist,...
items.fullDescription: Between XVII.34 (2027): Resonances and Polysemy: Musical Forms and Meanings in the Literary Text. Editors : Stefano Franceschini (Roma Tre University), Fiorenzo Iuliano (University of Cagliari) Submission Deadline: 27 May 2027 Publication Date: 15 December 2027 In Chapter 25 of Thomas Mann's Doctor Faustus (1947), Mephistopheles promises the protagonist, Adrian Leverkühn, twenty-four years of uninterrupted musical creativity in exchange for his soul, assuring him that he will "in drunken indulgence taste every bliss of almost intolerable infusion" and that, "in certain wanton moments," he may "plainly and honestly deem himself a god." Attracted yet alarmed by such an offer, the young composer asks to know the details of the transaction. Mephistopheles replies: "You would have knowledge of the pernicies, of the confutatio? […] one may use and fashion a great many words, yet all of them are but representative, stand for names that do not exist, can make no claim to designate that which can never ever be designated and denounced in words. That is the secret delight and security of hell, that it cannot be denounced, that it lies hidden from language." The devil refers to the inadequacy of language when faced with something as elusive as the essence of hell. The same can be said of music as the art of the ineffable, as Augusto Romano defines it in Musica e psiche (2021). Too often, however, the ineffable tends to be equated with the meaningless, what cannot convey any meaning at all: music, in other words, would possess no expressive means beyond a recursive exercise in self-reference (Hanslick 1854). This perspective, confining musical meaning within the boundaries of the work itself, has been challenged by approaches emphasizing music's capacity to produce historical and cultural meanings that cannot be reduced to formal principles alone (Kramer 2001). Yet one need only consider artistic practices such as program music and film scores, the entire range of discourses centered on music - from interpretive analysis and aesthetic-philosophical treatises to reviews and literary works - as well as the far more subjective experiences of musical transport, whether emotional, imaginative, or synesthetic, which have also been widely debated, to see how difficult it is to sustain the understanding of music as a system characterized by mere semio-phenomenal processes. Although its roots lie in a much older tradition, the relationship between literature and music acquired renewed prominence with modernism, on both the thematic and formal levels. Literature, and fiction in particular, increasingly turned to music as a thematic and structural model (Bucknell 2001; Wolf 1999). If, on the one hand, technological and industrial innovations around the turn of the twentieth century profoundly transformed access to music in domestic spaces - through the spread first of the phonograph and subsequently of radio (Sterne 2003), later leading to modern sound reproduction systems - on the other, the expansion of increasingly noisy urban environments had a sociocultural impact that over time radically reshaped individual acoustic experience (Schafer 1977). Many writers have consequently devoted considerable attention to sound, and particularly to music, as a vehicle for aesthetic, historical, and cultural reflection: from E.T.A. Hoffmann's "Ritter Gluck" (1809) and Honoré de Balzac's "Gambara" (1837), through Lev Tolstoy's Krejcerova sonata (1889), E.M. Forster's Howards End (1910), Aldous Huxley's Point Counter Point (1928), and Mann's aforementioned Doctor Faustus , to Marguerite Duras's Moderato cantabile (1958), Alejo Carpentier's Concierto barroco (1974), Thomas Bernhard's Der Untergeher (1983), Pascal Quignard's Tous les matins du monde (1991), Toni Morrison's Jazz (1992), Roberto Controneo's Presto con fuoco (1995), Vikram Seth's An Equal Music (1999), Richard Powers's The Time of Our Singing (2003), Moisés Kaufman's 33 Variations (2007), Claudio Morandini's Rapsodia su un solo tema. Colloqui con Rafail Dvoinikov (2010), Mathias Énard's Compass (2017), and Jenny Erpenbeck's Kairos (2021), to name but a few. What strategies can a written text employ to represent music? Can a literary text identify and illuminate a network of musical meanings? To what extent can different literary forms - narrative, poetry, and drama - incorporate such meanings into their structures and distinctive expressive modes, making music available to characters and other textual components as a means through which to reflect upon and intervene in reality? This issue of Between aims to explore the forms and modes through which literature, in its various expressions - fiction, poetry, and drama - engages with music, understood not simply as a theme or object of representation, but as a language, a means of knowledge, and a potential principle of formal organization. How does a literary text evoke, rework, recode, or reconstruct musical experience? How can it incorporate musical syntax - rhythm, melody, harmony, tonality, forms, and compositional procedures - and turn it into a means of producing new meanings? From this perspective, the relationship between music and literature may be approached on formal and aesthetic as well as historical, social, and political grounds. Music can contribute to the construction of subjectivities and identities; organize temporality and memory; define generational, cultural, or national affiliations; shape space and everyday experience; or provide a terrain on which the literary text can reflect upon its own limits and its expressive and epistemological possibilities. At the same time, the encounter between word and music raises broader questions concerning intersemiotic translation, intermediality, and the relationships between different systems of signification. The issue welcomes theoretical and methodological contributions as well as studies devoted to individual authors, works, or corpora, with particular emphasis on comparative approaches. Proposals that combine formal analysis with attention to the specific historical, cultural, and media conditions within which musical experience is produced, received, and reworked are especially welcome. Possible areas of inquiry include, but are not limited to: - music as a means for the production and articulation of meaning in literary texts; - musical forms, structures, and practices in the construction of literary texts: rhythmic organization, counterpoint, polyphony, variation, thematic development, serialism, and improvisation; - forms and functions of composition, performance, and listening in literary texts; - music, memory, and affect; - music as a means of interpreting historical, social, and political processes; - technologies of musical composition, recording, reproduction, and circulation and their interaction with literature; - voice and vocality between literature and music; - intersemiotic translation, intermediality, musical ineffability, and the limits of verbal representation. Authors are invited to consult the selected bibliography provided at the end of the call for papers. For questions or further information, please contact the editors at the email addresses ( stefano.franceschini@uniroma3.it and iuliano@unica.it ). Articles ready for publication, not exceeding 40,000 characters including spaces and formatted according to the provided template, with title, abstract, and metadata in English, must be submitted to the journal by 27 May 2027 , following the instructions available on the Submissions page of the Between website (Please note that the Between Journal website is currently under maintenance. Further submission details will be available starting in November 2026). Accepted articles will be published on 15 December 2027 . Contributions are accepted in Italian, English, and French, as well as in bilingual versions. Submissions in a language other than Italian, or in a bilingual version in which one of the languages is English or French, are particularly welcome and encouraged. items.title: Call for Journal Articles: AI and Religion
items.excerpt: We are pleased to invite you to contribute to a Special Issue of Religions examining how religious traditions, communities, and imaginaries shape the ways people design, interpret, and live with artificial intelligence (AI). Historians of technology have long observed that Western industrial cultures carry theological aspirations toward transcendence and...
items.fullDescription: We are pleased to invite you to contribute to a Special Issue of Religions examining how religious traditions, communities, and imaginaries shape the ways people design, interpret, and live with artificial intelligence (AI). Historians of technology have long observed that Western industrial cultures carry theological aspirations toward transcendence and redemption (Noble 1997). Geraci (2010) traced how apocalyptic hopes for mind uploading and machine superintelligence migrated from popular science into research laboratories and funding agendas. More recent scholarship examines how people attribute providence to recommendation algorithms, consult chatbots as spiritual advisors, and debate whether an artificial system can bear the image of God (Herzfeld 2023; Singler 2024). In hospitals and clinics, predictive models now issue forecasts about disease and mortality that patients and physicians receive with a deference once reserved for oracles (Furiasse 2026). These developments show that religion remains an active participant in the making of AI, supplying the metaphors, temporal frameworks, and moral vocabularies through which engineers, users, and critics make sense of these systems. This Special Issue aims to gather scholarship that treats religious traditions as sources of theory for understanding AI. Contributors are invited to ask how theological, ritual, mythic, and prophetic categories illuminate the design, marketing, and everyday use of AI systems, and how religious communities adapt, resist, or reimagine these technologies in their own practice. The issue fits the scope of Religions as an interdisciplinary journal publishing work on religion across the humanities, philosophy, and the social sciences. We welcome contributions from comparative religion, theology, anthropology, history, philosophy, media studies, and science and technology studies. We especially encourage perspectives from Africana, Indigenous, Asian, and other traditions that remain underrepresented in current debates about AI (Hui 2016). In this Special Issue, original research articles and reviews are welcome. Research areas may include, but are not limited to the following topics. Theological anthropology and the question of machine personhood Prophecy, divination, and religious framings of predictive algorithms in medicine, finance, and governance Apocalyptic, millenarian, and transhumanist narratives in the technology industry Critical analysis of ritual uses of chatbots, AI companions, and digital avatars of the dead, exploring questions of use, reception, ethics, governance, and authority Religious communities' adoption of, and resistance to, AI in worship, pastoral care, and education Religious and theological imaginaries of AI intimacy, companionship, and desire in popular media and the religious imagination Indigenous, Africana, and Asian cosmotechnics and alternative AI futures Religious ethics and the governance of AI systems Sacred texts, translation, and large language models By bringing scholars of religion into conversation with researchers in technology studies and the health sciences, the issue seeks to establish religious thought as a resource for evaluating AI and for imagining more accountable alternatives. Dr. Amanda Furiasse Guest Editor Deadline for Submissions: June 30, 2027 Manuscript Submission Information: Manuscripts should be submitted online at Religions: https://www.mdpi.com/journal/religions/special_issues/30370G3K21 Contact Information Amanda Furiasse, PhD Associate Professor of Medical and Digital Humanities Department of Humanities and Politics Nova Southeastern University Contact Email afuriass@nova.edu

items.title: Classical Echoes: Performing the Influence of Ancient Greek and Roman Literature
items.excerpt: Special Issue Website: https://www.mdpi.com/journal/literature/special_issues/B781Q58SAM Dear Colleagues, This Special Issue of Literature will collect essays addressing the reception, influence, adaptation, or incorporation of literature from the Greco-Roman world into later theatre, film, and television. The Greeks and Romans pioneered a wide range of p...
items.fullDescription: Special Issue Website: https://www.mdpi.com/journal/literature/special_issues/B781Q58SAM Dear Colleagues, This Special Issue of Literature will collect essays addressing the reception, influence, adaptation, or incorporation of literature from the Greco-Roman world into later theatre, film, and television. The Greeks and Romans pioneered a wide range of performed literary styles like tragic and comic drama, or epic and lyric poetry, as well as developing extensive mythic story networks and what we now recognize as formal histories, etc. Some of these works remain among the most influential and beloved writings ever produced by humanity. Because Greco-Roman literature is so culturally powerful and beloved, receptions and uses of it have occurred continually since the Greco-Roman era itself, in myriad different ways. This Issue seeks articles focused on performed receptions, exploring the cultural and artistic politics of how Greco-Roman material is brought to life for viewers, either on stages or screens. The recent controversies about casting and "historical accuracy" with Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey film remind us of the power and perils of live performance in the evocation of classics, so the articles for this Issue will interrogate the weight of and responses to classics' cultural authority. The Special Issue aims to provide current scholarly arguments about the role and ongoing power of Greek and Roman literature in theatre, film, television, or other performed media, consistent with the broader aims and scope of Literature. Purposefully taking a broad lens, the Issue seeks essays focused across time periods (e.g., medieval to the present), different national or regional performances/arts, and across media in order to bring together the most comprehensive body of essays possible. Potential topics include, but are not limited to: Theatrical or performed adaptation of or allusions to Greek and Roman literature within the Greco-Roman world. Medieval European or Middle Eastern reworkings and influence of Greco-Roman poetry or drama. Renaissance or Enlightenment re-conceptualizations of classical works. Re-writings, reworkings, artistic depictions, stagings, etc., of Greek or Roman literature for popular audiences (including Nolan's recent film). Global receptions and performances of Greco-Roman literature for postcolonial or comparative literature purposes. Feminist performed engagement with and critique of classics. Dr. Phillip Zapkin Guest Editor Manuscript Submission Information Manuscripts should be submitted online at www.mdpi.com by registering and logging in to this website. Once you are registered, click here to go to the submission form. Manuscripts can be submitted until the deadline. All submissions that pass pre-check are peer-reviewed. Accepted papers will be published continuously in the journal (as soon as accepted) and will be listed together on the special issue website. Research articles, review articles as well as short communications are invited. For planned papers, a title and short abstract (about 250 words) can be sent to the Editorial Office for assessment. Submitted manuscripts should not have been published previously, nor be under consideration for publication elsewhere (except conference proceedings papers). All manuscripts are thoroughly refereed through a double-anonymized peer-review process. A guide for authors and other relevant information for submission of manuscripts is available on the Instructions for Authors page. Literature is an international peer-reviewed open access quarterly journal published by MDPI. Please visit the Instructions for Authors page before submitting a manuscript. The Article Processing Charge (APC) for publication in this open access journal is 1000 CHF (Swiss Francs). Submitted papers should be well formatted and use good English. Authors may use MDPI's English editing service prior to publication or during author revisions. Keywords: Greek Roman literature reception adaptation studies classics

items.title: evolution/technology/culture
items.excerpt: Dear Colleagues , On behalf of the Editorial Board of Er(r)go: Theory - Literature - Culture (100 points on the Polish Ministry of Science and Higher Education journal ranking; indexed in Scopus; Gold Open Access), as Guest Editors, we are pleased to invite you to submit contributions to the forthcoming issue of the journal: 57 (2/2028) - evolution/techno...
items.fullDescription: Dear Colleagues , On behalf of the Editorial Board of Er(r)go: Theory - Literature - Culture (100 points on the Polish Ministry of Science and Higher Education journal ranking; indexed in Scopus; Gold Open Access), as Guest Editors, we are pleased to invite you to submit contributions to the forthcoming issue of the journal: 57 (2/2028) - evolution/technology/culture Guest edited by Piotr Gorli?ski-Kucik, Jerzy Stachowicz, and Weronika Nawrocka Submission deadline: 15 September 2027 https://journals.us.edu.pl/index.php/ERRGO/announcement/view/297 Submission link: https://journals.us.edu.pl/index.php/ERRGO/about/submissions How are we to think of evolution beyond biology today? And how can we avoid reducing it to the banal metaphor of progress? The development of civilization in the first decades of the twenty-first century has fostered an intensification of apocalyptic and dystopian modes of thought-yet this by no means precludes thinking in evolutionary terms. On the contrary: evolutionary thinking may offer a particularly productive way of describing ambiguous trends and sudden transformations. Evolutionism remains an indispensable component of modern social imaginaries, even when it is not always recognized or explicitly named as such. Evolution may be understood either as a gradual process or as an organizing principle governing transformations within complex systems, while evolutionism may be conceived as a body of methods and concepts employed to describe transformations in society, culture, and technology. The distinction, therefore, is between evolution as an object of inquiry and evolutionism as an analytical framework for describing processes of change. While Darwinism remains the dominant paradigm within the natural sciences, both transformist approaches and Lamarckism may prove intellectually generative within the humanities and social sciences. The phenomenon and discourse of evolution should be examined in relation to materialism, which conceives of evolution as an immanent process devoid of telos, as well as to new materialism, within which evolution may be understood as an ontology of the differentiation of forms, as the ceaseless production of zoe, and matter itself as living and self-organizing within a relational process of becoming. Other perspectives, however, are equally significant: within idealist or essentialist frameworks, evolution becomes inscribed within a broader metaphysical order. It is therefore also important to emphasize the connections between evolutionary theory and humanistic reflection on the nature and development of technology. The connections between evolutionary theory and humanistic reflection on the development of technology became apparent as early as four years after the publication of On the Origin of Species, with Samuel Butler's famous essay Darwin among the Machines (1863). In recent years, the debate over the place of technology within concepts of evolutionary development has gained particular intensity amid the latest wave of interest in AI. In this context, especially significant are the links between evolutionism and quasi-religious forms of transhumanism, progressivism, and accelerationism, as well as the question of the role these formations may play in ideological legitimization of techno-capital. How, then, can we describe the relations between evolution, technology, and culture without reducing them to a simple logic of progress? Does evolution remain a category for describing transformation, or does it also become a means of legitimizing it? How does its meaning change in the context of "new new" media, post-literacy, and the Anthropocene? We invite scholars in philosophy, literary studies, and other disciplines concerned with contemporary cultural forms and practices to address these problems. Within the broader reflection on the relations between evolution/technology/culture, we welcome submissions addressing, among others, the following issues: philosophies of evolution and philosophies of evolutionism evolution as a category for describing transformations within complex systems the subject and object of evolution evolutionism in the service of ideology new materialism and evolution as a process of becoming technology: from the Enlightenment to artificial intelligence evolution as a mode of thought, imagination, and social imaginary metaphysical and essentialist approaches to evolution transformations of media, post-literacy, and modes of information exchange evolutionism as a framework for diagnosing trends and processes of civilizational change Manuscripts, together with all required metadata, should be submitted via the OJS system by 15 September 2027, in accordance with the procedures described in the "About the Journal" and "For Authors" sections. Submissions must include: The Author's full name The Author's institutional affiliation The Author's ORCID number (www.orcid.org) The Author's website address, if applicable The Author's email address If the Author wishes to receive a complimentary hard copy of the journal, the postal address to which the copy should be sent The title of the article An abstract of 250-350 words A biographical note on the Author of 250-350 words Keywords (conforming to the WoS and SCOPUS standards) The academic discipline(s) represented The text of the article prepared in strict accordance with the Chicago Manual of Style (4,000-6,000 words) A bibliography of works cited prepared in strict accordance with the Chicago Manual of Style All illustrative materials in print-quality resolution (minimum 300 dpi) In the case of copyrighted visual materials, all relevant permissions or licences obtained by the Author A signed declaration concerning the use of artificial intelligence in the preparation of the manuscript, submitted together with the article and all required metadata Declaration concerning the use of Artificial Intelligence (click here to download the form) IMPORTANT: Incomplete submissions will be automatically rejected. FOR DETAILED TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS, PLEASE CONSULT THE "FOR AUTHORS" SECTION. With kindest regards , Piotr Gorli?ski-Kucik, Jerzy Stachowicz, and Weronika Nawrocka
